a: So no descaler ends up in the coffee
89253.e: Leftover acidic descaler would make the coffee taste sour. That is why you run clean water through it several times afterwards.
89253.m: After descaling, rinse thoroughly with clean water.

89254.q: Why does more limescale form in appliances in some regions of Switzerland than in others?
a: Because the tap water there is harder
Because the air there is damper
Because the appliances there are older
89254.e: Water that flows through limestone takes up many calcium and magnesium ions and is hard. Hard water leaves more limescale.
89254.m: Hard water leaves more limescale than soft water.

89255.q: What does it mean when tap water is ‘hard’?
a: It contains a lot of dissolved lime
89255.e: Hard water contains many dissolved calcium and magnesium particles. When it is heated, these form limescale.
89255.m: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved lime.

89256.q: Which kitchen ingredient can you use for descaling?
89256.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. This dissolves limescale, for example on shower heads or taps.
89256.m: Vinegar descales because it contains acetic acid.

89257.q: Why should you descale a coffee machine regularly?
a: Limescale blocks the pipes and makes heating less efficient
89257.e: Limescale builds up on heating elements and in thin pipes. The appliance then needs more energy and can get blocked.
89257.m: Limescale blocks appliances and wastes energy.

89258.q: Why should you not mix descaler with cleaners containing chlorine?
89258.e: Acids release poisonous chlorine gas from cleaners containing chlorine. That is why such products must never be used together.
89258.m: Never mix acidic cleaners with chlorine cleaners.

89259.q: Which organ does the acidic food mixture go to directly after the stomach?
89259.e: After the stomach comes the small intestine. There the acid is neutralised and the food is digested further.
89259.m: After the stomach, the food mixture goes into the small intestine.

89260.q: Which pH is typical for stomach juice when the stomach is empty?
89260.e: In an empty stomach, the stomach juice is strongly acidic. After eating, the pH rises a little because the food buffers the acid.
89260.m: Stomach juice is strongly acidic in an empty stomach.

89261.q: What is one of the jobs of stomach acid?
a: It kills many germs in food
89261.e: The strongly acidic conditions in the stomach kill many bacteria that enter the body with food. It also helps with digestion.
89261.m: Stomach acid protects against many germs from food.

89262.q: Which nutrient is partly digested in the stomach with the help of acid and the enzyme pepsin?
89262.e: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin. Pepsin splits proteins into smaller pieces.
89262.m: The digestion of proteins begins in the stomach.

89263.q: Why does the stomach not digest itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall
The stomach wall is made of metal
The acid is neutral in the stomach
The stomach completely renews itself every second
89263.e: The stomach lining makes a thick mucus that covers the wall. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
89263.m: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

a: Stomach acid gets into the gullet
Too much water in the gut
89264.e: When acidic stomach contents flow back into the gullet, they irritate its lining. You feel a burning behind the breastbone.
89264.m: With heartburn, stomach acid rises into the gullet.

89265.q: What kind of substance helps against too much stomach acid?
89265.e: Basic substances neutralise acids. That is why remedies for heartburn contain basic compounds.

89266.q: Where in the body is the acidic stomach juice made?
89266.e: Special cells in the stomach lining, the parietal cells, release hydrochloric acid. Other cells make mucus and enzymes.
89266.m: Stomach acid is made by cells in the stomach lining.

89267.q: Below roughly what pH do we speak of acid rain?
89267.e: Even clean rain is slightly acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; its pH is about 5.6. If it is lower, we speak of acid rain.
89267.m: Rain with a pH below about 5.6 counts as acid rain.

89268.q: Which gas from burning coal and heating oil contributes especially to acid rain?
89268.e: Coal and heating oil contain sulphur. Burning them produces sulphur dioxide, which turns into sulphuric acid in the air.
89268.m: Sulphur dioxide from coal and oil causes acid rain.

89269.q: Which gases from car engines also contribute to acid rain?
89269.e: In hot engines, nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides. In the air these form nitric acid.
89269.m: Nitrogen oxides from engines form nitric acid in the air.

89270.q: Which damage caused by acid rain did people in Switzerland debate especially hotly in the 1980s?
89270.e: In the 1980s, people argued intensely about damage to trees under the slogan ‘forest dieback’. Acid rain counted as an important cause.
89270.m: Acid rain started the debate about forest dieback in the 1980s.

89271.q: Why are marble statues worn away especially badly by acid rain?
a: Marble is made of lime, which is dissolved by acids
Marble dissolves in water like sugar
89271.e: Like limestone, marble is made of calcium carbonate. Acids slowly dissolve it, so statues lose their details.
89271.m: Acid rain eats away buildings made of limestone and marble.

89272.q: Which measure greatly reduced acid rain in Europe?
a: Filters that remove sulphur from exhaust gases
89272.e: Flue gas desulphurisation in power stations and low-sulphur fuels greatly cut the release of sulphur dioxide. Since then rain has been much less acidic.
89272.m: Removing sulphur from exhaust gases has greatly reduced acid rain.

89274.q: What can happen to fish in lakes that have become very acidic from acid rain?
a: They can die because the water is too acidic
89274.e: Many kinds of fish can only cope with slightly acidic water. In very acidic lakes in Scandinavia, whole fish populations died for this reason.

89275.q: How can you tell that an acid is reacting with limestone?
a: It fizzes and forms gas bubbles
The stone gets hot and glows
89275.e: The reaction produces a gas. The bubbles make the acid fizz on the stone.
89275.m: Limestone fizzes when it comes into contact with acid.

89276.q: How do geologists test in the field whether a rock contains lime?
a: They drip dilute hydrochloric acid on it
They put it in salt water
They hold a magnet to it
89276.e: If the rock fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, it contains calcium carbonate. This is called the acid test.
89276.m: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used to test rock for lime.

89277.q: What is the chemical formula of calcium carbonate, the main part of limestone?
89277.e: Calcium carbonate is made of calcium ions and carbonate ions (CO3). This gives the formula CaCO3.
89277.m: Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate, with the formula CaCO3.

89278.q: What happens to the shell of a raw egg if you leave the egg in vinegar for a day?
89278.e: Eggshells are mainly calcium carbonate. The acetic acid dissolves the shell, and only the soft skin is left.
89278.m: Vinegar dissolves eggshells, which contain lime.

89279.q: Which rock forms when limestone is changed deep in the Earth by heat and pressure?
89279.e: Under great heat and high pressure, limestone is changed into marble. That is why marble, like limestone, is made of calcium carbonate.

a: Water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves the limestone
Volcanoes blast holes in the rock
89280.e: Rainwater takes in carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic. Over a long time it dissolves the lime and forms hollow spaces.
89280.m: Slightly acidic water dissolves limestone and so forms caves.

89281.q: Which of these substances is also mainly made of calcium carbonate?
89281.e: Chalk, limestone and marble are all mainly made of calcium carbonate. Granite and quartz, on the other hand, are mainly made of silicates.
89281.m: Like limestone, chalk is made of calcium carbonate.

89282.q: Which household product removes limescale from a kettle?
89282.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. The acid dissolves the limescale, and bubbles of carbon dioxide form.
89282.m: Acids such as vinegar dissolve limescale.

89283.q: Which fruits contain especially large amounts of citric acid?
89283.e: Citrus fruits such as lemons and limes contain a lot of citric acid. It gives them their sour taste.
89283.m: Lemons and limes are rich in citric acid.

89284.q: What is citric acid often used for in the home?
89284.e: Citric acid dissolves limescale. That is why it is used to descale kettles and coffee machines.

89285.q: What does pure citric acid look like at room temperature?
89285.e: Pure citric acid is a colourless to white solid. You buy it as a powder, for example for descaling.
89285.m: Pure citric acid is a white powder.

89286.q: With which living thing is most citric acid made industrially today?
89286.e: Today citric acid is mainly made from sugar using the mould Aspergillus niger. Lemons alone could not meet the demand.
89286.m: Citric acid is made industrially with moulds.

89287.q: What are the salts of citric acid called?
89287.e: The salts and esters of citric acid are called citrates. One example is sodium citrate, which is found in foods.
89287.m: The salts of citric acid are called citrates.

89288.q: What is the citric acid cycle in our cells for?
89288.e: In the citric acid cycle, cells get energy from nutrients. Citric acid is an important substance along the way.
89288.m: The citric acid cycle supplies cells with energy.

89289.q: Why can citric acid remove limescale from a kettle?
a: The acid makes the limescale magnetic
The acid makes the limescale invisible
89289.e: Acids react with limescale. The limescale dissolves and can be rinsed away.
89289.m: Acids such as citric acid dissolve limescale.

89290.q: Where did citric acid come from in the past, before people made it with moulds?
89290.e: In the 18th century, citric acid first came from lemon juice. Today it is mainly made from sugar using moulds.
89290.m: Citric acid was first obtained from lemon juice.

89291.q: Where is ammonia often used as a refrigerant?
a: In artificial ice rinks and large cold stores
89291.e: In large cooling systems such as artificial ice rinks, ammonia is a proven refrigerant. Because it is poisonous, it is hardly used in small household appliances.
89291.m: Large cooling systems such as ice rinks are often cooled with ammonia.

89292.q: What does ammonia gas smell like?
89292.e: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a very sharp smell. You may know the smell from badly aired stables.
89292.m: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp smell.

89293.q: What is a solution of ammonia in water like?
a: Different depending on the time of day
89293.e: In water, ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion. This produces hydroxide ions and the solution becomes alkaline.
89293.m: Ammonia forms an alkaline solution with water.

89294.q: What is the well-known process for making ammonia on a large scale called?
89294.e: At the beginning of the 20th century, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a process for making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
89294.m: Ammonia is made by the Haber-Bosch process.

89295.q: What is most of the ammonia produced used for?
89295.e: Nitrogen fertiliser is made from ammonia. Without this fertiliser, far fewer people in the world could be fed.
89295.m: Ammonia is the raw material for nitrogen fertiliser.

89296.q: What was the old name for a solution of ammonia in water, often used in the past as a cleaning agent?
89296.e: Spirit of hartshorn is ammonia dissolved in water. Ammonia solution is used, for example, in glass cleaners.
89296.m: Spirit of hartshorn is a solution of ammonia in water.

89297.q: Which ion forms when ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion?
89297.e: Ammonia (NH3) takes up a hydrogen ion and becomes the ammonium ion (NH4+). Ammonium salts are found in many fertilisers.
89297.m: Ammonia and a hydrogen ion make the ammonium ion.

89298.q: Is ammonia gas lighter or heavier than air?
89298.e: Ammonia has a lower density than air. That is why escaping ammonia rises upwards.
89298.m: Ammonia gas is lighter than air.

89299.q: Which form of energy of dammed water is used in a storage power station?
89299.e: Water stored high up has potential energy. As it flows down, this turns into movement energy, which drives turbines.
89299.m: Storage power stations use the potential energy of water dammed up high.

89300.q: Roughly how much of Switzerland's electricity comes from hydropower?
89300.e: Hydropower supplies around 60 per cent of Switzerland's electricity. It is the most important home-grown source of electricity.
89300.m: More than half of Swiss electricity comes from hydropower.

89301.q: What is a hydroelectric power station on a river called that uses the flowing water without a large reservoir?
89301.e: Run-of-river power stations stand on rivers such as the Rhine or the Aare. They produce electricity round the clock from the water flowing past.
89301.m: Run-of-river power stations use river water directly.

89302.q: Which part of a hydroelectric power station turns the turbine's rotation into electrical energy?
89302.e: The turbine is connected to a generator. Inside it, a magnet turns in coils, which produces electric current.
89302.m: The generator turns rotation into electricity.

89303.q: Why are many storage power stations in the Alps?
a: The water falls a very long way there
89303.e: In the Alps, reservoirs lie high above the power stations. The greater the drop, the more energy there is in the water.
89303.m: Big drops make the Alps ideal for hydropower.

89304.q: Which part of a hydroelectric power station is driven by the water and turns?
89304.e: The water flows through the turbine and makes it turn. The turbine then drives the generator.

89305.q: Which two cantons produce the most electricity from hydropower?
89305.e: The mountain cantons of Valais and the Grisons have many reservoirs and big drops. Together they produce a large share of Swiss hydropower.
89305.m: Valais and the Grisons are Switzerland's biggest hydropower cantons.

89306.q: Why is hydropower from reservoirs especially valuable for the electricity supply?
a: The electricity can be produced when it is needed
89306.e: The water in the reservoir waits until it is needed. So production can be quickly raised and lowered, for example in winter or at peak times.
89306.m: Reservoirs store energy that is turned into electricity when needed.

89307.q: Why are pumped storage power stations becoming more important as solar and wind power expand?
a: They can store the changing electricity from sun and wind
They only work when it is windy
89307.e: Sun and wind do not always supply electricity when it is needed. Pumped storage takes in surpluses and releases them later.
89307.m: Pumped storage evens out the ups and downs of solar and wind power.

89308.q: Because of what it does, what is a pumped storage power station often called?
89308.e: Like a battery, it can take in energy and release it later. That is why people speak of a “water battery”.
89308.m: A pumped storage power station works like a giant battery.

89309.q: Why do you get less electricity back from a pumped storage power station than you put in for pumping?
a: Some energy is lost in the pumps and turbines
The lake gives the energy to the fish
89309.e: Friction in pipes, pumps, turbines and generators turns some of the energy into heat. Overall you get back about three quarters to four fifths.
89309.m: Pumped storage gives back less energy than was needed for pumping.

89310.q: In which canton is the Nant de Drance pumped storage power station, which started operating in 2022?
89310.e: Nant de Drance is near Finhaut in Lower Valais. It uses the Emosson and Vieux Emosson reservoirs.
89310.m: The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station is in Valais.

89311.q: What is the Nant de Drance pumped storage power station known for?
a: It is one of the most powerful pumped storage plants in Europe
It is the oldest power station in Switzerland
It stands in the middle of the city of Geneva
89311.e: Nant de Drance has six machine units with a total output of 900 megawatts. So it can supply or store a lot of electricity very quickly.
89311.m: Nant de Drance is one of Europe's most powerful pumped storage plants.

89312.q: Where are the machines of Nant de Drance?
a: In a cavern deep inside the mountain
On a raft on the reservoir
In a tower block in Martigny
Under a glass dome on the summit
89312.e: The turbines and pumps are in a huge rock cavern in the mountain between the two reservoirs. There they are protected and can hardly be seen from outside.
89312.m: The machines of Nant de Drance work in a cavern inside the mountain.

89313.q: In which canton is the Linth-Limmern pumped storage power station, with the Muttsee as its upper reservoir?
89313.e: Linth-Limmern is in the canton of Glarus. The water is pumped back and forth between Lake Limmern and the higher Muttsee.
89313.m: The Linth-Limmern pumped storage power station is in the canton of Glarus.

89314.q: What is the smallest number of reservoirs or basins a pumped storage power station needs?
89314.e: It needs an upper and a lower basin at different heights. The water is sent back and forth between them.
89314.m: A pumped storage power station needs an upper and a lower basin.

89315.q: When does a pumped storage power station typically let the water flow through the turbines?
a: When a lot of electricity is needed
When the sun is very strong and there is plenty of electricity
Only when the lake is frozen
89315.e: When demand is high, for example in the evening, the water is let down. The turbines then produce extra electricity.
89315.m: When demand is high, a pumped storage power station produces electricity.

89316.q: Which process supplies the heat in a nuclear power station?
89316.e: In the reactor, uranium nuclei are split by neutrons. This releases a lot of heat, which is used to turn water into steam.
89316.m: Nuclear power stations get heat from splitting uranium nuclei.

89317.q: How many nuclear reactors were operating in Switzerland in 2025?
89317.e: Beznau 1 and 2, Gösgen and Leibstadt were operating (as of 2025). A fifth plant has already been shut down and is being dismantled.
89317.m: Switzerland has four nuclear reactors in operation (as of 2025).

89318.q: Which Swiss nuclear power station was shut down for good in December 2019?
89318.e: The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was taken off the grid on 20 December 2019. Since then it has been dismantled.
89318.m: The Mühleberg nuclear power station was shut down in 2019.

89319.q: What rises as a white cloud from the cooling tower of a nuclear power station?
89319.e: In the cooling tower, cooling water is cooled by evaporation. The visible cloud is made of condensed water vapour.
89319.m: The cloud above a cooling tower is water vapour.

89320.q: In which canton are the Beznau and Leibstadt nuclear power stations?
89320.e: Beznau is near Döttingen and Leibstadt is on the Rhine, both in the canton of Aargau. Gösgen is in the canton of Solothurn.
89320.m: Beznau and Leibstadt are in the canton of Aargau.

89321.q: Where is the radioactive waste from Swiss nuclear power stations meant to go one day?
a: Into a store deep in the rock
89321.e: Nagra is planning a deep geological repository. There the waste is to be safely sealed in solid rock many hundreds of metres down.
89321.m: Radioactive waste is to be stored deep in the rock.

89322.q: Which energy conversion takes place in the steam turbine of a nuclear power station?
a: The energy of the steam becomes rotation
89322.e: Hot steam at high pressure flows through the turbine and makes it turn. This rotation is then converted into electric current.
89322.m: In the steam turbine, hot steam drives a rotation.

89323.q: Which event in 2011 led the Federal Council to decide on a gradual exit from nuclear power?
89323.e: After the accident at the Fukushima nuclear power station in Japan in March 2011, the Federal Council decided not to build any new nuclear power stations. The existing ones are to be shut down at the end of their working lives.
89323.m: After Fukushima in 2011, Switzerland decided on a gradual nuclear exit.

89324.q: Which is the newest and most powerful nuclear power station in Switzerland?
89324.e: Leibstadt started operating in 1984 and has an output of around 1200 megawatts. It is the largest nuclear power station in Switzerland.
89324.m: Leibstadt is the largest nuclear power station in Switzerland.

89325.q: What is the water of the Lac des Dix mainly used for?
89325.e: The water flows through tunnels and pressure pipes down into the Rhône valley. There it drives turbines in hydroelectric power stations.
89325.m: The water of the Grande Dixence generates electricity.

89326.q: What is the reservoir behind the Grande Dixence dam called?
89326.e: The Grande Dixence holds back the Lac des Dix in the upper Val d'Hérémence. By volume it is the largest reservoir in Switzerland.
89326.m: The Lac des Dix lies behind the Grande Dixence.

89327.q: In which canton is the Grande Dixence?
89327.e: The dam is in the Val d'Hérémence, a side valley south of Sion in the canton of Valais.
89327.m: The Grande Dixence is in the canton of Valais.

89328.q: How does a gravity dam like the Grande Dixence hold back the water?
a: With steel cables to the mountain tops
With pumps that push against the water
With an arch that sends the pressure into the rock walls
89328.e: The wall is very wide at the base and extremely heavy. Its weight stops the water pressure from pushing it away.
89328.m: A gravity dam resists the water with its weight.

89329.q: Where does some of the water for the Lac des Dix come from?
a: It is pumped from valleys as far as Zermatt
89329.e: Pumping stations such as Zmutt and Stafel near Zermatt send glacier water into a network of tunnels. That way water from several valleys reaches the reservoir.
89329.m: The Grande Dixence collects water from many valleys in Valais, even from the Zermatt area.

89330.q: What building material is the Grande Dixence dam made of?
89330.e: Around 6 million cubic metres of concrete were used for the wall. For years the concrete was brought to the site by cable cars and cranes.
89330.m: The Grande Dixence dam is made of concrete.

89331.q: Roughly at what height is the highest water level of the Lac des Dix?
89331.e: The maximum water level is at 2364 metres above sea level. Because it is so high, the water has a lot of potential energy on its way down to the Rhône valley.
89331.m: The Lac des Dix lies at about 2360 metres above sea level.

89332.q: In which unit is the output of a solar power system given?
89332.e: Power is measured in watts or kilowatts. A solar system on a family house often has a peak output of around 10 kilowatts.
89332.m: The output of a solar system is measured in kilowatts.

89333.q: What material are most solar cells made of?
89333.e: Most solar cells are made of crystalline silicon, a semiconductor. Silicon is obtained from quartz sand.
89333.m: Most solar cells are made of silicon.

89334.q: Which device turns the direct current from solar panels into alternating current for the household mains?
89334.e: Solar panels supply direct current. The inverter turns it into alternating current at 50 hertz, like the current in the power grid.
89334.m: The inverter turns solar direct current into alternating current.

89335.q: Roughly what share of Swiss electricity production did solar power have in 2024?
89335.e: According to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, solar power supplied about 7.4 per cent of the electricity produced in Switzerland in 2024. Its share is growing clearly every year.
89335.m: In 2024 solar power supplied about 7 per cent of Swiss electricity.

89336.q: Why do solar systems in the Alps produce more electricity in winter than in the Central Plateau?
a: They are above the fog and the snow reflects extra light
The sun is closer in the mountains
More rain falls in the cold
In the mountains the sun shines at night too
89336.e: In winter you are often above the fog in the Alps. The snow also reflects light, and cold solar cells work more efficiently.
89336.m: Alpine solar systems supply a lot of electricity in winter.

89337.q: What is the difference between photovoltaics and solar thermal energy?
a: Photovoltaics produces electricity, solar thermal produces heat
89337.e: Photovoltaic panels produce electric current. Solar thermal collectors, on the other hand, heat water, for example for the shower or heating.
89337.m: Photovoltaics supplies electricity, solar thermal supplies heat.

89338.q: In which direction should solar panels ideally face in Switzerland to produce the most electricity over the year?
89338.e: In Switzerland the sun is in the south at midday. Panels tilted towards the south therefore get the most light over the year.
89338.m: In Switzerland, south-facing solar panels produce the most electricity.

89339.q: Why was a large solar system built on the Muttsee dam at around 2500 metres?
a: Because it produces a lot of electricity there in winter
Because the sun never sets there
Because power stations are not allowed there
89339.e: The AlpinSolar project in the canton of Glarus is often above the fog, and the snow reflects extra light. That is why the system supplies especially a lot of winter electricity.
89339.m: Alpine solar systems like the one at the Muttsee supply lots of winter electricity.

89340.q: Roughly what share of Swiss electricity production did wind power have in 2024?
89340.e: According to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, wind power's share in 2024 was around 0.2 per cent. So far there are only a few large wind turbines in Switzerland.
89340.m: Wind power supplies less than one per cent of Swiss electricity so far.

89341.q: What problem do wind turbines high in the Alps have especially in winter?
a: Ice builds up on the rotor blades
89341.e: In cold and fog, ice can form on the rotor blades. That is why some turbines, for example on the Gütsch above Andermatt, have blade heating.
89341.m: In the mountains, ice on wind turbines can be a problem.

89342.q: Why are wind turbines in Switzerland often built on Jura ridges and mountain passes?
a: The wind blows more strongly and steadily there
89342.e: In valleys the wind is slowed down. On ridges and passes it blows more strongly and regularly, which brings more electricity.
89342.m: Wind turbines stand where the wind blows strongly and regularly.

89343.q: How many rotor blades do most large modern wind turbines have?
89343.e: Three blades are a good compromise: the rotor runs smoothly, is stable and makes good use of the wind.
89343.m: Large modern wind turbines usually have three rotor blades.

a: Several wind turbines in the same place
A park where it is always windy
89345.e: In a wind farm several wind turbines stand together. In Switzerland there are wind farms in the Jura and at the Nufenen Pass, for example.
89345.m: A wind farm is made up of several wind turbines.

89346.q: What happens to a wind turbine in a very strong storm?
a: It is switched off to avoid damage
It turns as fast as it can
It is folded down to the ground
89346.e: Above a certain wind speed the rotor blades are turned out of the wind. This protects the turbine from overload.
89346.m: In a storm wind turbines are switched off for protection.

89347.q: Which form of the wind's energy does a wind turbine use?
89347.e: Moving air has kinetic energy. The rotor takes some of it and turns it into rotation, from which electricity is produced.
89347.m: Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of the air.

89348.q: Which gas is the main part of biogas?
89348.e: Biogas is usually about half to two thirds methane. The rest is mainly carbon dioxide.
89348.m: The main burnable part of biogas is methane.

89349.q: What is biogas often produced from on farms?
89349.e: Slurry and manure contain a lot of organic material. Bacteria break it down into biogas in closed tanks.
89349.m: Biogas can be made from slurry and manure.

89350.q: Under what conditions do bacteria break down the biomass in a biogas plant?
89350.e: The fermentation in the digester takes place with no air. Only then do the bacteria produce methane.
89350.m: Biogas forms when bacteria break down biomass without oxygen.

89351.q: What is the tank called in which fermentation takes place in a biogas plant?
89351.e: In the digester the biomass is kept warm and stirred. There the bacteria break down the material and form gas.
89351.m: Fermentation in a biogas plant takes place in the digester.

89352.q: What does a combined heat and power plant running on biogas produce?
89352.e: An engine burns the biogas and so produces electricity. The waste heat from the engine is also used for heating.
89352.m: A combined heat and power plant supplies electricity and heat at the same time.

89353.q: What is often done with the leftovers from a farm biogas plant?
a: They are burnt in the fireplace
89353.e: The leftovers still contain many nutrients. They are spread on fields and used as fertiliser.
89353.m: Leftovers from biogas plants are used as fertiliser.

89354.q: What is biogas called that has been cleaned and can be fed into the natural gas grid?
89354.e: For the gas grid the carbon dioxide is removed. What is left is almost pure methane, called biomethane.

89355.q: In which plants is sewage gas, a form of biogas, produced?
89355.e: The sludge from the waste water is fermented in digestion towers. This produces sewage gas, which is often used for electricity and heat.
89355.m: Sewage plants make biogas from sewage sludge.

89356.q: Where does an air-to-water heat pump get its heat from?
89356.e: The heat pump draws heat from the outside air, even at temperatures below zero. This heat is raised to a higher temperature and used for heating.
89356.m: An air-to-water heat pump uses the heat in the outside air.

89357.q: Which household appliance is a heat pump technically closely related to?
89357.e: A fridge pumps heat from its inside to the outside. A heat pump does the same, only it brings the heat from outside into the house.
89357.m: A heat pump works like a fridge in reverse.

89358.q: A heat pump makes about 4 kilowatt hours of heat from 1 kilowatt hour of electricity. Where does the rest come from?
a: From the surroundings, for example the air or ground
From the refrigerant, which gets used up
From the water in the heating
89358.e: The heat pump takes most of the heat from the environment. The electricity only drives the compressor.
89358.m: A heat pump gets most of its heat from the environment.

89359.q: What is the borehole called that a heat pump uses to get heat from underground?
89359.e: For a ground probe, a pipe is often sunk well over 100 metres deep into the ground. A liquid in it takes up the heat of the ground.
89359.m: A ground probe gets heat from underground.

89360.q: What energy does a heat pump need to run?
89360.e: The heat pump needs electricity to drive its pump for the refrigerant. But most of the heating warmth comes from the environment.

89361.q: Which substance circulates in a heat pump and evaporates even at low temperatures?
89361.e: The refrigerant takes up heat from the environment in the evaporator and turns into a gas. Then it is brought to a higher temperature and gives its heat to the heating.
89361.m: In a heat pump a refrigerant carries the heat.

89362.q: Which part of a heat pump compresses the gaseous refrigerant and so raises its temperature?
89362.e: When you squeeze a gas together, it gets warm. The compressor uses this to raise the temperature for the heating.
89362.m: In a heat pump the compressor raises the refrigerant's temperature.

89363.q: Why are heat pumps considered better for the climate than oil heating?
a: They burn no heating oil and use heat from the environment
They need no energy at all
They cool the house in winter
89363.e: Burning oil for heating produces a lot of carbon dioxide. A heat pump uses heat from the environment and electricity, most of which is produced with low CO2 in Switzerland.
89363.m: Heat pumps heat without burning heating oil.

a: A digital electricity meter that sends usage data automatically
A measuring tape for power lines
89364.e: A smart meter measures electricity use continuously and sends the data automatically to the grid operator. In Switzerland the old meters are gradually being replaced by these smart meters.
89364.m: A smart meter is an intelligent, digital electricity meter.

89365.q: What voltage does a normal socket in Switzerland supply?
89365.e: At the end of the power grid, an alternating voltage of 230 volts reaches the household. Before that, the high voltage is lowered step by step in transformers.

89366.q: What is meant by a blackout?
a: A widespread power cut lasting a long time
89366.e: In a blackout the electricity fails over a large area, often for hours. Transport, communication and the water supply are affected too.
89366.m: A blackout is a widespread power cut.

89367.q: Why is electricity sent over long distances at very high voltage?
a: Because then the losses in the lines are smaller
Because then the electricity arrives faster
Because high voltage is cheaper to measure
Because then birds do not land
89367.e: At high voltage, less current flows for the same power. That means the lines heat up less and less energy is lost.
89367.m: High voltage reduces losses when transporting electricity.

89368.q: Which device in the power grid changes the voltage, for example from high voltage to 230 volts?
89368.e: Transformers are made of coils on an iron core. Depending on the number of turns, they raise or lower the voltage.
89368.m: Transformers raise or lower the voltage in the power grid.

89369.q: What does Swissgrid's transmission network carry across Switzerland?
89369.e: Swissgrid runs Switzerland's extra-high-voltage grid. It connects the big power stations with the regions and the neighbouring countries.
89369.m: Swissgrid runs the Swiss extra-high-voltage grid.

89370.q: Why is the Swiss power grid connected to the grids of neighbouring countries?
a: So that countries can exchange electricity and help each other out
So that the electricity becomes coloured
So that no power stations are needed any more
So that the electricity flows more slowly
89370.e: Through these connections Switzerland can import and export electricity. If a power station fails somewhere, the other grids help out.
89370.m: The Swiss power grid is connected to the whole of Europe.

89371.q: What must be true in the power grid at every moment so that the frequency stays stable?
a: Production and consumption must be equal
All power stations must run at the same time
Consumption must be twice as big as production
Electricity may only flow at night
89371.e: If more is used than produced, the frequency drops; in the opposite case it rises. That is why power stations are constantly adjusted.
89371.m: In the power grid, production and consumption must always be in balance.

89372.q: Who decided on the new Energy Act in Switzerland in 2017?
89372.e: On 21 May 2017 around 58 per cent of voters said yes to the new Energy Act. This started the implementation of the Energy Strategy 2050.
89372.m: In 2017 the people said yes to the Energy Strategy 2050.

89373.q: What can you do in everyday life to help with the goals of the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: Switch off the light when you leave the room
Turn the heating up high with the window open
Leave the TV on all the time
Always take the car for short trips
89373.e: The Energy Strategy 2050 wants less energy to be wasted. Every light switched off and every trip on foot saves energy.
89373.m: Saving energy helps the Energy Strategy 2050.

89374.q: What are the three main goals of the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: Save energy, expand renewable energy, gradually replace nuclear power
Burn more coal, import more oil, export more electricity
Empty all reservoirs, take down wind turbines, make petrol cheaper
Use only nuclear power and ban solar panels
89374.e: The strategy relies on more energy efficiency and expanding hydropower, solar, wind and biomass. This is meant to replace the electricity from the nuclear power stations that are shut down.
89374.m: The Energy Strategy 2050 relies on efficiency and renewable energy.

89375.q: Which federal office is mainly responsible for implementing the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE)
The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)
89375.e: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy is part of the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (DETEC). It looks after energy policy and publishes the energy statistics.
89375.m: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy implements the Energy Strategy 2050.

89376.q: What did the Federal Council decide in 2011 after the nuclear accident at Fukushima in Japan?
a: A gradual exit from nuclear power
To build many new nuclear power stations
89376.e: After the accident at Fukushima, the Federal Council under Energy Minister Doris Leuthard decided not to build any new nuclear power stations. This led to the Energy Strategy 2050.
89376.m: After Fukushima, Switzerland decided to exit nuclear power.

89377.q: What is the law for a secure electricity supply from renewable energy that the people accepted in June 2024 called?
89377.e: On 9 June 2024 around 69 per cent of voters accepted the so-called Electricity Act. It is meant to speed up the expansion of hydro, solar and wind power.
89377.m: The Electricity Act accepted in 2024 promotes the expansion of renewable energy.

89378.q: Which climate goal for 2050 did the voters accept in 2023 with the Climate and Innovation Act?
a: Twice as much heating oil as today
89378.e: On 18 June 2023 the people accepted the Climate and Innovation Act. By 2050 Switzerland is to emit no more greenhouse gases overall.
89378.m: Switzerland aims to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

a: Getting the same benefit with less energy
Using as much energy as possible
89379.e: An efficient appliance needs less energy for the same result, for example an LED lamp instead of a light bulb. Efficiency is a pillar of the Energy Strategy 2050.
89379.m: Energy efficiency means achieving the same with less energy.

89380.q: Roughly how much electricity was used in Switzerland in 2024 (final consumption)?
89380.e: According to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, electricity consumption in 2024 was 57.5 terawatt hours. One terawatt hour is a billion kilowatt hours.
89380.m: In 2024 Switzerland used about 57 terawatt hours of electricity.

89381.q: In which unit is electricity use shown on the electricity bill?
89381.e: The kilowatt hour measures energy. It shows how much electricity was used over a certain time.
89381.m: Electricity use is measured in kilowatt hours.

89382.q: A 2000-watt kettle runs for 3 hours in total. How much energy does it use?
89382.e: 2000 watts are 2 kilowatts. 2 kW times 3 h makes 6 kWh.
89382.m: Energy is calculated as power times time.

89383.q: One kilowatt hour costs 30 centimes. How much do 6 kWh cost?
89383.e: 6 times 30 centimes makes 180 centimes. That is 1.80 francs.
89383.m: Electricity costs are usage times the price per kilowatt hour.

89384.q: In which season is electricity use in Switzerland highest?
89384.e: In winter more light and heating energy is needed, for example for heat pumps. At the same time rivers and solar systems supply less electricity.
89384.m: Switzerland uses the most electricity in winter.

89385.q: What does the energy label on a fridge show?
a: How economical the appliance is with energy
89385.e: The energy label puts appliances into classes from A to G. Class A stands for the most economical appliances.
89385.m: The energy label shows how economical an appliance is.

89386.q: What is the electricity use of an appliance called that seems to be switched off but is still plugged in?
89386.e: Many appliances wait on standby for a signal from the remote control and use a little electricity all the time for this. A switchable power strip helps you save.
89386.m: Appliances on standby use electricity too.

89387.q: Why does an LED lamp use less electricity than a light bulb of the same brightness?
a: It turns more energy into light and less into heat
It only shines half as long
It needs no electricity at all
It is smaller and therefore more economical
89387.e: A light bulb turns most of the electricity into heat. LED lamps produce much more light per watt.
89387.m: LED lamps are more economical because they lose less energy as heat.

a: Heat produced centrally and delivered to many buildings through pipes
Heat from the sun in space
Heat from an electric heater in the living room
89388.e: A heating plant or a facility with waste heat heats water. This flows through well-insulated pipes to the connected houses.
89388.m: District heating is produced centrally and distributed through pipes.

89389.q: Which plants supply a large part of the district heating in many Swiss cities?
89389.e: Burning rubbish produces a lot of heat. Waste incineration plants use it for electricity and district heating.
89389.m: Waste incineration plants supply lots of district heating.

89390.q: In what form is the heat carried in most district heating networks?
a: As hot water in insulated pipes
As hot air in ventilation shafts
89390.e: Hot water or steam flows to the houses in a supply pipe. The cooled water returns to the plant in a return pipe.
89390.m: District heating mostly flows as hot water through insulated pipes.

89391.q: What advantage does a house connected to district heating have over a house with its own oil heating?
a: It needs no boiler and no oil tank of its own
It needs no radiators at all
The flat automatically stays cool in summer
It no longer has a water connection
89391.e: Instead of a boiler there is only a small transfer station in the basement. An oil tank and chimney are no longer needed.
89391.m: With district heating a house needs no boiler of its own.

89392.q: What is the part called that passes the heat from the district heating network to the house's own heating without the water mixing?
89392.e: In the heat exchanger, the water from the network and the house's heating water flow separately side by side. The heat passes through thin metal walls.
89392.m: A heat exchanger passes on heat without the liquids mixing.

89393.q: What can the waste heat from a power station usefully be used for?
89393.e: Power stations produce a lot of heat that would otherwise be lost. Through a district heating network it can heat nearby houses, for example at the Beznau nuclear power station.
89393.m: Waste heat from power stations can heat houses.

89394.q: Which fuel is used in many rural heating networks in Switzerland?
89394.e: Wood chips from Swiss forests are burnt in central heating plants. The heat is then distributed to the connected buildings.
89394.m: Many heating networks use wood chips from the region.

a: Heat produced as a by-product of a process
Heat that is turned off at night
Heat that you buy in a shop
89395.e: Waste heat is produced in factories or data centres, for example. Instead of letting it escape unused, it can be used through district heating networks.
89395.m: Waste heat is heat produced as a by-product that can be put to use.

89396.q: In propositional logic, what is meant by a proposition?
a: A sentence that is either true or false
A sentence that is always true
A question with exactly two answers
A sentence with no truth value at all
89396.e: By the principle of bivalence, every proposition has exactly one of the two truth values true or false. Questions or commands are therefore not propositions.
89396.m: A proposition is either true or false.

89397.q: Which connective is false only when the premise is true and the conclusion is false?
89397.e: The implication A → B (“if A, then B”) is only violated if A holds but B does not. In all other cases it is true.
89397.m: An implication is only false when something false follows from something true.

89398.q: According to De Morgan’s laws, which formula is equivalent to ¬(A ∧ B)?
89398.e: A conjunction is false exactly when at least one of its parts is false. So when negating, “and” becomes “or”, and both parts are negated.
89398.m: Negating an and-connection turns it into an or-connection of the negated parts.

89399.q: What do you call a formula of propositional logic that is true for every assignment of the variables?
89399.e: A tautology such as A ∨ ¬A is true purely because of its logical form. Its truth value does not depend on whether A is true or false.
89399.m: A tautology is a formula that is always true.

89400.q: Which formula is logically equivalent to the implication A → B (contraposition)?
89400.e: If B always follows from A, B cannot be false while A is true. So ¬A always follows from ¬B. The converse B → A, however, is not equivalent.
89400.m: The contrapositive of an implication swaps and negates both parts.

89401.q: When is the disjunction A ∨ B (the inclusive or) true?
a: When at least one part is true
When exactly one part is true
Only when both parts are true
89401.e: The logical or includes the case where both parts are true. A ∨ B is only false when A and B are both false.
89401.m: The logical or is already true when one of the two statements is true.

89402.q: Which connective is true exactly when both parts have the same truth value?
89402.e: The equivalence A ↔ B (“if and only if”) is true when A and B are both true or both false. It corresponds to two implications in both directions.
89402.m: The equivalence is true when both statements are equally true or equally false.

89403.q: What do you call a formula like A ∧ ¬A that is false for every assignment?
89403.e: A statement and its negation can never both be true. So A ∧ ¬A is always false and is called a contradiction.
89403.m: A contradiction is a formula that is always false.

89404.q: How many rows does a complete truth table with n propositional variables have?
89404.e: Each variable can be true or false. With n variables there are therefore 2 · 2 · … · 2 = 2^n combinations, so 2^n rows.
89404.m: With each additional variable the number of rows in a truth table doubles.

89405.q: In how many rows of the truth table with variables A and B is A ∧ B true?
89405.e: The table has 4 rows. The conjunction is only true in the row where A and B are both true.
89405.m: An and-connection is only true if all parts are true.

89406.q: In how many of the four rows of a truth table is A ∨ B true?
89406.e: Only in the row where A and B are both false is the or false. In the other three rows it is true.
89406.m: An or is only false if all parts are false.

89407.q: What is the truth value of A → B if A is false and B is true?
a: True and false at the same time
89407.e: If the premise is false, the implication is always true (“ex falso quodlibet”). It is only false when A is true and B is false.
89407.m: Any statement at all follows from a false premise.

89408.q: How many different two-place truth functions (connectives with two inputs) are there?
89408.e: A table with two variables has 4 rows. In each row the result can be true or false, so there are 2^4 = 16 possibilities.
89408.m: There are sixteen different two-place connectives.

89409.q: In how many of the four rows is the exclusive or (A XOR B) true?
89409.e: XOR is true when exactly one of the two statements is true. That applies to the rows “A true, B false” and “A false, B true”.
89409.m: The exclusive or requires exactly one statement to be true.

89410.q: In how many rows of the truth table is the formula (A ∧ B) → A false?
89410.e: For the implication to be false, A ∧ B would have to be true and A false. That is impossible, so the formula is true in all rows.
89410.m: A formula that is true in every row is universally valid.

89411.q: Which formula has exactly the same result column in the truth table as A → B?
89411.e: ¬A ∨ B is only false if ¬A is false (so A is true) and B is false. That is exactly how the implication behaves.
89411.m: The implication can be written as “not A or B”.

89412.q: How do you show with a truth table that two formulas are logically equivalent?
a: You compare their result columns row by row
You only check the first row
You count the variables of both formulas
You compare the length of the formulas
89412.e: Two formulas are equivalent if they have the same truth value for every assignment. If the columns match in all rows, this is shown.
89412.m: Equivalent formulas have the same truth value in every row.

89413.q: How does a proof by contradiction begin?
a: You assume the opposite of the claim
You first prove the case n = 1
89413.e: In an indirect proof the negation of the claim is assumed. If this assumption leads to a contradiction, the claim must be true.
89413.m: A proof by contradiction starts by assuming the opposite.

89414.q: What is the Latin name for proof by contradiction?
89414.e: “Reductio ad absurdum” means “reduction to the absurd”. The assumption is shown to be absurd.
89414.m: Proof by contradiction is called “reductio ad absurdum” in Latin.

89415.q: Which logical principle is proof by contradiction essentially based on?
a: The law of the excluded middle
89415.e: Either a statement is true or its negation is true; there is no third possibility. Once the negation is disproved, only the statement itself remains.
89415.m: With no third possibility, the statement follows from its disproved negation.

89416.q: For a proof by contradiction you assume √2 is a fully reduced fraction p/q. What contradiction follows from this?
a: p and q would both be even
p and q would both be odd
89416.e: From √2 = p/q it follows that p² = 2q², so p is even. Substituting p = 2k gives q² = 2k², so q is even too. Then the fraction would not be fully reduced, a contradiction.
89416.m: The classic proof by contradiction shows that √2 cannot be a fraction.

89417.q: How do you show indirectly that there is no largest natural number?
a: For a supposedly largest number n, n + 1 would be even larger
You show that 0 is the smallest number
89417.e: Suppose n is the largest natural number. Then n + 1 is also a natural number and larger than n, which contradicts the assumption.
89417.m: For every natural number there is a larger one.

89418.q: What must you have found at the end of a proof by contradiction?
a: A statement that would have to hold together with its opposite
A statement that cannot be checked
89418.e: From the assumption, a statement and its negation are logically derived. Because both cannot be true at once, the assumption is false.
89418.m: A proof by contradiction ends with a statement that contradicts its own opposite.

89419.q: If you assume log₂(3) is the fraction p/q with natural numbers p and q, it follows that 2^p = 3^q. Why is this a contradiction?
a: The left side is even, the right side odd
Both sides would be prime numbers
p and q would have to be equal
The left side would be negative
89419.e: For p ≥ 1, 2^p is even, while every power of 3 is odd. A number cannot be even and odd at the same time, so log₂(3) is irrational.
89419.m: A power of two can never equal a power of three.

89420.q: How do you show indirectly that there is no smallest positive rational number?
a: For a supposedly smallest number r, r/2 is even smaller and also positive and rational
You show that 1 is the smallest positive number
You calculate r · 2 and get a larger number
89420.e: If r were the smallest positive rational number, r/2 would be positive, rational and smaller than r. That contradicts the assumption.
89420.m: For every positive rational number there is a smaller positive rational number.

89421.q: What characterises the decimal representation of an irrational number?
a: It is infinitely long and not recurring
It ends after finitely many digits
It has at most ten decimal places
89421.e: Rational numbers have terminating or recurring decimals. Irrational numbers have infinitely many decimal places with no repeating pattern.
89421.m: Irrational numbers have infinitely many decimal places without a repeating pattern.

89422.q: What is true of the product of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number?
a: It is always a whole number
89422.e: If r · x were rational, then x = (r · x) / r would also be rational as a quotient of two rational numbers. That contradicts x being irrational.
89422.m: Multiplying an irrational number by a non-zero rational number keeps it irrational.

89423.q: Is the sum of two irrational numbers always irrational?
a: No, it can also be rational
Only for positive numbers is it rational
Only for roots is it rational
89423.e: A counterexample is √3 + (−√3) = 0. Zero is rational, even though both terms are irrational.
89423.m: The sum of two irrational numbers can be rational.

89424.q: In 1882 it was proved that π is transcendental. Which old problem was finally solved by this?
a: Squaring the circle with compass and straightedge is impossible
π can be written as a fraction
89424.e: A square with the same area as a unit circle would need side length √π. Because π is transcendental, this length cannot be constructed with compass and straightedge. The proof was given by Ferdinand von Lindemann.
89424.m: Squaring the circle is impossible because π is transcendental.

89425.q: What did the scholar Johann Heinrich Lambert, born in Mulhouse, prove about the number π in the 18th century?
a: That π is a recurring decimal
89425.e: Lambert (1728 to 1777) was the first to prove, in 1761 using continued fractions, that π is irrational. His home town of Mulhouse was then allied with the Swiss Confederation.
89425.m: Lambert was the first to prove that π is irrational.

a: A number that is not a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients
A number larger than every natural number
A number with a recurring decimal representation
A number that can be written as a fraction
89426.e: Algebraic numbers are roots of polynomials with integer coefficients (other than the zero polynomial). All other real or complex numbers are called transcendental, for example e.
89426.m: Transcendental numbers are not a solution of any polynomial equation with integer coefficients.

89427.q: Roughly what is the value of the golden ratio, a well-known irrational number?
89427.e: The golden ratio is (1 + √5) / 2 ≈ 1.618. The other values belong to √2, e and π.

89428.q: For which natural numbers n is √n a rational number?
a: Only if n is a square number
Only if n is a prime number
89428.e: If √n is rational, it must even be a whole number. That is why √9 = 3 is rational, but √10 is irrational.
89428.m: The square root of a natural number is either a whole number or irrational.

89429.q: Which ancient school is credited with discovering incommensurable, that is irrational, ratios?
89429.e: According to tradition, the Pythagorean Hippasus of Metapontum discovered in the 5th century BC that some line segments have no common measure. This shook the teaching that everything is number.
89429.m: The Pythagoreans were the first to come across irrational ratios.

89430.q: You assume √2 = p/q with natural numbers p and q. What extra assumption does the classic proof make?
a: The fraction p/q is fully reduced
p and q are both prime numbers
89430.e: Every fraction can be fully reduced, so the assumption is allowed. It is exactly this that leads to the contradiction at the end.
89430.m: In the proof you assume that the fraction for √2 is already reduced.

89431.q: From √2 = p/q it follows that p² = 2q². What do you conclude from this first?
a: p² is even, so p is even too
89431.e: 2q² is obviously even. The square of an odd number is odd, so p itself must be even.
89431.m: If a square is even, the number itself is even too.

89432.q: In the proof you substitute p = 2k into p² = 2q². Which equation results?
89432.e: From (2k)² = 2q² it follows that 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k². So q² is even and therefore q is too.
89432.m: Substituting shows that q must be even as well.

89433.q: What is the final contradiction in the proof that √2 is irrational?
a: p and q would both be even, so the fraction would not be reduced
q would have to be zero
89433.e: If p and q are both even, p/q can still be reduced by 2. That contradicts the assumption of a fully reduced fraction.
89433.m: A fully reduced fraction cannot have a factor of 2 in both numerator and denominator.

89434.q: Which value approximates √2 to three decimal places?
89434.m: The square root of 2 is about 1.414.

a: As the diagonal of a square with side length 1
As the height of an equilateral triangle with side length 1
As the circumference of a circle with radius 1
As the space diagonal of a cube with edge length 1
89435.e: By Pythagoras, the diagonal d of a unit square satisfies d² = 1² + 1² = 2. The space diagonal of the unit cube, however, is √3.
89435.m: The diagonal of a unit square is √2 long.

89436.q: An alternative proof uses prime factorisation. How often does each prime factor appear in a square number p²?
89436.e: In p², each prime factor appears twice as often as in p. In 2q², however, the factor 2 appears an odd number of times, so p² = 2q² cannot hold.
89436.m: In a square number every prime factor appears an even number of times.

89437.q: Which culture already knew a very accurate approximation of √2 around 1800 BC, as a clay tablet shows?
89437.e: The Babylonian clay tablet YBC 7289 shows a square with diagonals and a value for √2 that is correct to about six decimal places. The Babylonians calculated in base 60.
89437.m: The Babylonians already knew very good approximations of √2.

a: Yes, it is a root of x² − 2
89438.e: √2 solves the equation x² − 2 = 0 with integer coefficients. So it is irrational but algebraic.
89438.m: The square root of 2 is irrational but algebraic.

89439.q: Why is the number N = p₁ · p₂ · … · pₙ + 1 crucial in Euclid’s proof, even though N itself need not be prime?
a: Every prime factor of N is missing from the assumed list
N is always a square number
N is divisible by all pᵢ
N is smaller than every pᵢ
89439.e: N > 1 has at least one prime factor. Because none of the primes p₁ to pₙ divides N, this prime factor must be new.
89439.m: Every number greater than one has a prime factor.

89440.q: In which work is Euclid’s proof about prime numbers found?
89440.e: The proof is in the ninth book of the “Elements” (Proposition 20). The work was a standard textbook for over 2000 years.
89440.m: Euclid’s “Elements” contain the proof about prime numbers.

89442.q: What remainder does the number p₁ · p₂ · … · pₙ + 1 leave when divided by one of the primes pᵢ?
89442.e: The product is divisible by each pᵢ, and the extra 1 remains. So none of the primes is a divisor.
89442.m: A product plus one is not divisible by any of its factors.

a: Yes, it is a prime number
89443.e: 30031 = 59 · 509. The proof does not require the number formed to be prime, only that its prime factor is new.
89443.m: The number from Euclid’s proof is not always a prime itself.

89444.e: Euclid probably worked in the 3rd century BC. Very little about his life is known for certain.

89445.q: According to tradition, in which city did Euclid work?
89445.e: Euclid is said to have taught in Alexandria in Egypt, the centre of Greek science at the time.

89446.q: Euclid proved that there are infinitely many primes. Which Basel mathematician, shown on the former 10-franc note, later found a completely different proof?
89446.e: Leonhard Euler (1707 to 1783) showed in 1737 that the sum of the reciprocals of all primes grows beyond all bounds. With finitely many primes this sum would be finite. Euler appeared on the 10-franc note of the sixth series.
89446.m: Euler gave an analytical proof that there are infinitely many primes.

89447.e: 17 = 3 · 5 + 2. So the remainder on division by 5 is 2.
89447.m: The mod operation gives the remainder of a division.

89448.q: It is 9 o’clock. What time is it 30 hours later?
89448.e: You calculate (9 + 30) mod 24 = 39 mod 24 = 15. So it is 15:00 the next day.
89448.m: Times of day are calculated modulo 24.

89449.q: Today is Monday. Which day of the week will it be in 100 days?
89449.e: 100 = 14 · 7 + 2. After 14 full weeks it is Monday again, two days later Wednesday.
89449.m: Days of the week are calculated modulo 7.

89450.q: What is the last digit of the number 7^100?
89450.e: The last digits of the powers of 7 repeat in the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1. Since 100 is divisible by 4, 7^100 ends in 1.
89450.m: The last digits of powers repeat in a fixed cycle.

89451.q: Which number is the multiplicative inverse of 3 modulo 7?
89451.m: Multiplied by a number, its inverse gives remainder 1.

89452.q: For which moduli m does every number from 1 to m − 1 have a multiplicative inverse modulo m?
a: When m is a prime number
When m is a square number
89452.e: A number a is invertible modulo m exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1. That holds for all a from 1 to m − 1 only when m is prime.
89452.m: Modulo a prime, every non-zero residue class is invertible.

89453.q: What remainder does 123456 leave when divided by 9?
89453.e: A number has the same remainder modulo 9 as its digit sum. 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21, and 21 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 9.
89453.m: Modulo 9, every number has the same remainder as its digit sum.

89454.q: What is the check digit in an IBAN, for example a Swiss IBAN, for?
a: It reveals typing errors in the number
It shows the year the account was opened
89454.e: The IBAN is converted into a long number which must give remainder 1 modulo 97. If a digit is mistyped, the remainder usually no longer matches.
89454.m: Checking an IBAN is based on calculating modulo 97.

89455.q: What does a ≡ b (mod m) mean?
a: m divides the difference a − b
a and b are both divisible by m
The product a · b equals m
The sum a + b equals m
89455.e: Two numbers are congruent modulo m if their difference is a multiple of m. Equivalently, they leave the same remainder when divided by m.
89455.m: Congruent numbers leave the same remainder when divided by the modulus.

89456.q: Who introduced the symbol ≡ for congruences in the “Disquisitiones Arithmeticae” in 1801?
89456.e: Gauss published the “Disquisitiones Arithmeticae” in 1801 at the age of 24. In it he founded modular arithmetic with the symbol ≡.
89456.m: Gauss introduced the notation for congruences.

89457.e: 38 − 14 = 24 is divisible by 12. For the others the difference 23, 21 or 14 is not divisible by the modulus.
89457.m: A congruence is correct if the difference is divisible by the modulus.

89458.q: What is the smallest positive solution of 2x ≡ 5 (mod 9)?
89458.e: Check: 2 · 7 = 14 = 9 + 5, so 14 ≡ 5 (mod 9). Smaller positive values of x do not satisfy the congruence.
89458.m: Linear congruences are solved using the inverse or by systematic trial.

89459.q: By the Chinese remainder theorem, which smallest positive number x satisfies x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 5)?
89459.e: 8 = 2 · 3 + 2 and 8 = 5 + 3. Because 3 and 5 are coprime, the solution is unique modulo 15.
89459.m: With coprime moduli, a system of congruences has exactly one solution per period.

89460.q: Suppose a ≡ b (mod m) and c ≡ d (mod m). What always follows?
89460.e: Congruences with the same modulus can be added, subtracted and multiplied term by term. So a · c ≡ b · d.
89460.m: You can multiply congruences just like equations.

89461.q: Which remainders can a square number leave when divided by 4?
89461.e: For even n = 2k, n² = 4k² ≡ 0; for odd n = 2k + 1, n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 ≡ 1 (mod 4).
89461.m: Square numbers only leave remainder 0 or 1 when divided by 4.

89462.q: Why does casting out nines work as a check on calculations?
89462.e: Every power of ten is congruent to 1 modulo 9. So a number is congruent to its digit sum modulo 9, and calculation errors often show up.
89462.m: Casting out nines relies on every power of ten leaving remainder 1 modulo 9.

89463.q: What does Fermat’s little theorem state for a prime p and an integer a?
a: a² + p² is a square number
89463.e: For every prime p and every integer a, a^p − a is divisible by p. For example 2^5 − 2 = 30 is divisible by 5.
89463.m: For every prime p, a to the power p minus a is divisible by p.

89464.q: Which condition does the form a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) of Fermat’s little theorem need?
a: a is not divisible by p
a is itself a prime number
89464.e: If a is divisible by p, then a^(p−1) ≡ 0. Only for coprime a may you cancel a and get remainder 1.
89464.m: The form with remainder 1 only holds if a is not divisible by p.

89465.q: What remainder does 3^100 leave when divided by 7?
89465.m: With Fermat’s little theorem you can reduce large exponents a lot.

89466.q: In which century did Pierre de Fermat formulate his little theorem?
89466.e: Fermat stated the theorem in 1640 in a letter to Frénicle de Bessy, without giving a proof. He lived from about 1607 to 1665.
89466.m: Fermat formulated the little theorem in the 17th century.

89467.q: Who was the first to publish a proof of Fermat’s little theorem?
89467.e: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz had a proof but did not publish it. Euler from Basel published the first proof in 1736 and later generalised the theorem.
89467.m: Euler published the first proof of Fermat’s little theorem.

89468.q: For a prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Conversely, does a^(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod n) always mean that n is prime?
a: No, some composite numbers satisfy it too
Yes, as soon as n is odd
No, because the formula only holds for a = 2
89468.e: For example 341 = 11 · 31 is not a prime, yet 2^340 ≡ 1 (mod 341). Such numbers are called pseudoprimes. So the converse of Fermat’s little theorem does not hold.
89468.m: The Fermat test cannot prove for certain that a number is prime.

89469.q: The Fermat test checks, for a number a with 1 < a < n, whether a^(n−1) leaves remainder 1 when divided by n. What follows for certain if the remainder is not 1?
a: n is certainly not a prime
Nothing at all can be concluded
89469.e: If n were prime, the remainder would have to be 1 by Fermat’s little theorem. So any other remainder proves that n is composite. Conversely, remainder 1 does not yet prove a prime.
89469.m: If a number fails the Fermat test, it is certainly not a prime.

89470.q: Which encryption method is based on a generalisation of Fermat’s little theorem?
89470.e: RSA uses Euler’s theorem, which generalises Fermat’s little theorem to any modulus. This shows that decryption gives back the message.
89470.m: The RSA method relies on the theorem of Euler and Fermat.

89471.q: Who is regarded as the founder of set theory?
89471.e: Georg Cantor developed set theory from about 1874. He particularly studied infinite sets and their sizes.

89472.q: How many elements does the set {∅, {∅}} have?
89472.e: The set contains the empty set and the set that contains only the empty set. Those are two different elements.
89472.m: The empty set can itself be an element of a set.

89473.q: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}. What is the intersection A ∩ B?
89473.e: The intersection contains exactly the elements that are in both sets. These are 3 and 4.
89473.m: The intersection contains only common elements.

89474.q: In a class of 25 pupils, 15 play football, 12 play floorball and 5 play both. How many play neither?
89474.e: By the inclusion-exclusion principle, 15 + 12 − 5 = 22 play at least one sport. So 25 − 22 = 3 play neither.
89474.m: With unions, you subtract what has been counted twice.

89475.q: Which paradox concerns “the set of all sets that do not contain themselves as an element”?
a: The paradox of Achilles and the tortoise
89475.e: Bertrand Russell showed in 1901: if this set contains itself, then it does not, and vice versa. This made an axiomatisation of set theory necessary.
89475.m: Russell’s paradox shows the limits of naive set theory.

89476.q: After Russell’s paradox, set theory was built on axioms. What is an axiom?
a: A basic statement assumed without proof
A statement confirmed by trial and error
A conjecture still to be proved
89476.e: Axioms are basic assumptions from which all further theorems are proved. Today’s usual foundation of set theory is the axiom system of Zermelo and Fraenkel.
89476.m: Axioms are the basic rules on which mathematics is built.

89477.q: What is the set of all subsets of a set M called?
89477.e: The power set P(M) contains every subset of M as an element. For M = {a, b}, P(M) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}}.
89477.m: The power set collects all subsets of a set.

89478.q: How many elements does the Cartesian product A × B have if A has 3 and B has 4 elements?
89478.e: A × B consists of all ordered pairs (a, b). There are 3 · 4 = 12 such pairs.
89478.m: The cardinality of a Cartesian product is the product of the cardinalities.

89479.q: What is the value of i², where i is the imaginary unit?
89479.e: The imaginary unit is defined so that its square is −1. This gives x² = −1 a solution.
89479.m: The square of the imaginary unit is minus one.

89480.e: Multiplying out gives 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i, because −3i² = +3.
89480.m: You multiply complex numbers like brackets and replace i² with minus one.

89481.q: What is the modulus of the complex number 3 + 4i?
89481.e: |3 + 4i| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. That is the distance from the origin of the complex plane.
89481.m: The modulus of a complex number is its distance from the origin.

89482.q: What is the value of i^2027?
89482.e: The powers of i repeat with period 4. 2027 = 506 · 4 + 3, so i^2027 = i³ = −i.
89482.m: The powers of i repeat every four steps.

89483.q: What is the complex conjugate of 4 − 7i?
89483.e: Conjugating only changes the sign of the imaginary part. In the complex plane this corresponds to a reflection in the real axis.
89483.m: Conjugating reverses the sign of the imaginary part.

89484.q: What is the real part of the complex number (1 + i)²?
89484.e: (1 + i)² = 1 + 2i + i² = 1 + 2i − 1 = 2i. The number is purely imaginary, so its real part is 0.
89484.m: A purely imaginary number has real part zero.

89485.q: How many complex roots does a polynomial of degree 5 have, counted with multiplicity?
89485.e: By the fundamental theorem of algebra, every polynomial of degree n splits into n linear factors over the complex numbers.
89485.m: A polynomial of degree n has exactly n complex roots counted with multiplicity.

89486.q: What are the solutions of x² + 9 = 0 in the complex numbers?
89486.e: From x² = −9 it follows that x = ±√9 · i = ±3i. Check: (3i)² = 9i² = −9.
89486.m: Negative numbers have two square roots in the complex numbers.

89487.q: What does it mean if a set is countably infinite?
a: It has the same cardinality as the natural numbers
It has only finitely many elements
It has the same cardinality as the set of all points on a line
89487.e: A countably infinite set can be mapped bijectively onto the natural numbers. So its elements can be numbered.
89487.m: A countably infinite set can be numbered without gaps.

89488.q: Which of these sets is uncountable?
89488.e: The real numbers cannot be numbered, so there is no bijection onto the natural numbers. Integers, even numbers and primes, however, are countable.

89489.q: With which method did Cantor show in 1891 that infinite sequences of digits are uncountable?
89489.e: For any supposedly complete list you form a sequence that differs from the nth sequence in the nth place. This sequence is missing from the list.
89489.m: With the diagonal argument you find a missing element for every list.

89490.q: In Hilbert’s Hotel, with infinitely many occupied rooms, a new guest arrives. How do you make room?
a: Every guest moves from room n to room n + 1
The new guest is turned away
Every guest moves from room n to room n − 1
89490.e: After the move, room 1 is free and all previous guests still have a room. An infinite set can have the same cardinality as a proper subset.
89490.m: An infinite set can be as large as a proper part of itself.

89491.q: What surprising discovery did Georg Cantor make about infinite sets?
a: There are infinities of different sizes
All infinite sets are the same size
89491.e: Cantor showed that the real numbers cannot be numbered, but the natural numbers can. So the real numbers form a larger infinity.
89491.m: According to Cantor there are infinities of different sizes.

89492.q: Which symbol denotes the cardinality of the natural numbers?
89492.e: Cantor used the Hebrew letter aleph. ℵ₀ is the smallest infinite cardinal number.
89492.m: The cardinality of the natural numbers is called aleph null.

a: Yes, all fractions can be numbered in a list
No, they have the same cardinality as ℝ
Only the positive fractions are countable
89493.e: If you arrange the fractions p/q in a grid and go through it diagonally, you reach every fraction. This is Cantor’s first diagonal method.
89493.m: Although the fractions are dense, they are countable.

89494.q: What does Cantor’s theorem show about a set M and its power set P(M)?
a: P(M) always has strictly greater cardinality than M
P(M) always has the same cardinality as M
89494.e: There is no surjective map from M onto P(M). It follows that there are infinitely many different infinite cardinalities.
89494.m: The subsets of a set are always strictly more numerous than its elements.

89495.q: Which of these infinite sets has the same cardinality as the natural numbers?
89495.e: Assigning the even number 2n to each natural number n gives a bijection. The other sets are uncountable.
89495.m: There are just as many even numbers as natural numbers.

89496.q: Which data does the Swiss Data Protection Act protect?
89496.e: The Data Protection Act sets out how information relating to a specific or identifiable person is handled. This includes things like name, address or photos.
89496.m: The Data Protection Act protects information about people.

89497.q: Under the Swiss Data Protection Act, what must a company do if it collects data about you?
a: Report the data to your school
89497.e: Companies have a duty to inform. They must say which data they collect and what they use it for.
89497.m: Anyone who collects personal data must inform the people concerned.

89498.q: What is the job of the FDPIC in Switzerland?
89498.e: FDPIC stands for Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner. It checks whether authorities and companies comply with the Data Protection Act and advises the public.
89498.m: The FDPIC watches over data protection in Switzerland.

89499.q: Which of these details counts as particularly sensitive under the Data Protection Act?
89499.e: Particularly sensitive data includes data about health, religion, political views, as well as genetic and biometric data. Stricter rules apply to it.
89499.m: Health data is particularly sensitive personal data.

89500.q: Under the Data Protection Act, what can you ask of a company that stores data about you?
a: Information about which data it has on you
A payment for every detail stored
The deletion of all data of all customers
89500.e: Everyone has a right of access. The company must say which data it processes about that person and why.
89500.m: You may ask which data a company has stored about you.

89501.q: What does it usually cost to ask a company which data it has about you?
a: Nothing, the information is usually free
A fee for each detail stored
You have to buy a yearly subscription
89501.e: The right of access is meant to be open to everyone. That is why the information is free in principle and usually has to be given within 30 days.
89501.m: Information about your own data is usually free.

89502.q: What can happen if someone deliberately breaks the Swiss Data Protection Act?
a: They can get a large fine
They only have to change their password
89502.e: For deliberate breaches there are fines of up to 250,000 francs. It is mainly the responsible people who are fined.
89502.m: Breaking data protection rules can be expensive.

89503.q: What does “privacy by default” mean in the Data Protection Act?
a: The most privacy-friendly setting is switched on from the start
All data is public by default
You have to choose a new password every year
Apps may only be used in Switzerland
89503.e: Default settings must be chosen so that only as little data as necessary is processed. Anyone who wants to share more has to set this up themselves.
89503.m: An app's basic settings should give away as little data as possible.

89504.q: What must a company do if personal data is stolen from it and this creates a high risk for the people concerned?
a: Report the incident to the FDPIC
Only inform the police in another country
89504.e: If there is a data security breach likely to cause a high risk, it must be reported to the FDPIC. The FDPIC should be informed as quickly as possible.
89504.m: A company must report serious data breaches to the FDPIC.

89505.q: Which English word does “phishing” come from?
89505.e: The fraudsters “fish” for passwords. The “ph” instead of “f” is a nod to earlier hacker spellings.
89505.m: In phishing, fraudsters fish for passwords.

89506.q: An email seems to come from your bank and asks for your password. What is correct?
a: Genuine banks never ask for passwords by email
You reply straight away with the password
You send only half of the password
You forward the email to all your friends
89506.e: Banks and other genuine companies never ask for passwords by email, text message or telephone. A request like this is almost always an attempt at fraud.
89506.m: No genuine company asks for your password by email.

89507.q: What is the best way to check where a link in a suspicious email really leads?
a: Hover the mouse over it without clicking and look at the address
89507.e: When you hover over it, the email program shows the real destination address. If it differs from the official address, be careful.
89507.m: Before clicking, you check where a link really leads.

89508.q: A phishing email knows your name and your school. Why is it particularly dangerous?
a: It can set the computer on fire
It definitely comes from the school
89508.e: Fraudsters collect information about their victim beforehand. A personal message seems believable, so it is easier to fall for it. This is called spear phishing.
89508.m: Personal phishing emails are especially hard to spot.

89509.q: Which federal office in Switzerland can you report cyber attacks such as phishing to (as of 2026)?
a: The Federal Office for Cyber Security
The Federal Office of Public Health
89509.e: The Federal Office for Cyber Security (NCSC) receives reports of cyber incidents. It grew out of the National Cyber Security Centre at the beginning of 2024.
89509.m: In Switzerland you can report cyber incidents to the Federal Office for Cyber Security.

89510.q: What is the general term for harmful programs?
89510.e: Malware is short for “malicious software”, meaning harmful software. Viruses, worms and Trojans all belong to it.
89510.m: Malware is the umbrella term for harmful programs.

89511.q: What is a harmful program called that spreads by itself over networks without attaching itself to a file?
89511.e: A computer worm uses networks and security gaps to copy itself from computer to computer. A virus, on the other hand, needs a host file.
89511.m: A worm spreads by itself over networks.

a: It secretly spies on data and behaviour
89512.e: Spyware collects information without the user knowing, such as websites visited or login details, and sends it to third parties.
