90154.e: In English, a low is called “Low” and a high “High”. That is why the maps show L and H. German maps use T for “Tief”.
90154.m: English weather maps show lows with an L.

90155.q: In what parts is cloud cover given on weather maps?
90155.e: Meteorology divides the sky into eight parts, called oktas. 0 oktas is cloudless, 8 oktas is completely overcast.
90155.m: Cloud cover is given in eighths.

90156.q: What does a weather map in the weather forecast show?
a: The weather over a large area at the same time
The weather in one single place
The weather in a hundred years
90156.e: For a weather map, measurements from many places taken at the same time are brought together. This lets you see highs, lows and fronts.
90156.m: A weather map shows the weather of many places at the same time.

90157.q: What does an isobar on a weather map connect?
a: Places with the same air pressure
Places with the same amount of rain
90157.e: Isobars are lines along which the air pressure is the same everywhere. They show where the highs and lows are.
90157.m: Isobars connect places with the same air pressure.

90158.q: What does it mean when the isobars on a weather map are very close together?
90158.e: Isobars close together show a big pressure difference over a short distance. The air then flows quickly, and it gets stormy.

90159.q: What does the Greek word “isos” in the term isobar mean?
90159.e: “Isos” means equal and “baros” means weight. So an isobar is a line of equal weight, meaning equal pressure.
90159.m: Isobar means line of equal pressure.

90160.q: What do the isobars around a high look like on a weather map?
a: Closed rings with values rising towards the inside
Straight lines from north to south
90160.e: Around a high, the isobars form closed curves. The highest pressure value is in the middle.
90160.m: Isobars lie like rings around a high.

90161.q: How do the numbers on the isobars change as you get closer to the centre of a low?
90161.e: In the centre of a low, the air pressure is lowest. So the values of the isobars decrease towards the inside.
90161.m: Towards the centre of a low, isobar values fall.

90162.q: High up, how does the wind blow compared with the isobars?
90162.e: The Earth’s rotation deflects the air so that high up it flows almost along the isobars. Near the ground, friction slows it, and the wind blows at an angle into the low.
90162.m: High up, the wind blows almost along the isobars.

90163.q: On a weather map, isobars are drawn at intervals of 5 hPa. What is the pressure difference between the first and the fifth isobar?
90163.e: Between the first and the fifth isobar there are 4 gaps. 4 times 5 makes 20 hectopascals.
90163.m: The spacing of isobars shows fixed steps of pressure.

90164.q: Isobars show equal air pressure. What are the matching lines of equal temperature called?
90164.e: “Therm” stands for heat. Isotherms connect places with the same temperature.
90164.m: Lines of equal temperature are called isotherms.

90165.q: What does an exothermic reaction give off to its surroundings?
90165.e: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released, usually as heat. This makes the surroundings warmer.
90165.m: An exothermic reaction gives off heat to its surroundings.

90166.q: Which process is an exothermic reaction?
90166.e: Burning wood releases large amounts of heat and light. The surroundings get noticeably warmer.
90166.m: Every combustion is an exothermic reaction.

90167.q: What does the Greek prefix ‘exo’ in the word exothermic mean?
90167.e: ‘Exo’ means ‘outside’ or ‘out’ and ‘thermos’ means ‘warm’. So exothermic means that heat is given out.
90167.m: Exothermic means that heat goes out.

90168.q: Where are the products of an exothermic reaction in an energy diagram?
a: Not in the diagram at all
90168.e: The products contain less energy than the starting materials. The difference is given off to the surroundings.
90168.m: In exothermic reactions the products have less energy than the starting materials.

90169.q: What sign does the reaction enthalpy have in an exothermic reaction?
90169.e: The system loses energy to its surroundings. That is why the reaction enthalpy is given with a minus sign.
90169.m: In exothermic reactions, the reaction enthalpy is negative.

90170.q: Disposable hand warmers contain iron powder. Which reaction provides the heat?
90170.e: When you open the packet, the fine iron reacts with oxygen in the air. This rusting happens very fast and gives off heat.
90170.m: The rusting of iron is also an exothermic reaction.

90171.q: What do you notice when you mix dilute hydrochloric acid with dilute sodium hydroxide solution?
a: Nothing, the temperature stays the same
90171.e: The acid and the alkali neutralise each other. This neutralisation is exothermic and warms the solution.
90171.m: Neutralising an acid with an alkali releases heat.

90172.q: What is the highly exothermic thermite reaction of aluminium and iron oxide used for?
90172.e: The thermite reaction produces liquid iron at over 2000 °C. This can be used to join pieces of rail directly on the track.
90172.m: The hot iron from the thermite reaction is used to weld rails together.

90173.q: Why does a candle flame feel hot?
a: The wax takes in heat from the air
The air is compressed by light
90173.e: The wax reacts with oxygen. This releases energy as heat and light.
90173.m: A burning candle gives off energy as heat and light.

90174.q: What does an endothermic reaction do with energy?
90174.e: An endothermic reaction needs energy from its surroundings, for example heat or light. Without a supply of energy it does not continue.
90174.m: An endothermic reaction takes in energy from its surroundings.

90175.q: Where do plants get the energy for endothermic photosynthesis?
90175.e: Plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. The energy is stored in the sugar.
90175.m: Photosynthesis needs the energy of sunlight.

90176.q: Instant cold packs get cold after you snap them. What happens inside?
a: A salt dissolves and takes in heat
A gas burns in the bag
90176.e: Inside the bag a salt such as ammonium nitrate dissolves in water. This process takes in heat from the surroundings, so the pack gets cold.
90176.m: A process that takes in heat cools its surroundings.

90177.q: What sign does the reaction enthalpy have in an endothermic reaction?
a: It depends on the time of day
90177.e: The system takes in energy and afterwards has more energy than before. That is why the reaction enthalpy is positive.
90177.m: In endothermic reactions, the reaction enthalpy is positive.

90178.q: Where are the products of an endothermic reaction in an energy diagram?
90178.e: The products have stored the energy that was taken in. That is why they are higher than the starting materials.
90178.m: In endothermic reactions the products have more energy than the starting materials.

90179.q: Why must the kiln be heated strongly the whole time when making quicklime?
a: Lime gives off a lot of heat
90179.e: Limestone only breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide at around 900 °C. The reaction keeps taking in heat and stops without heating.
90179.m: Making quicklime needs a constant supply of heat.

90180.q: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. What happens if you switch the electricity off?
90180.e: The electrolysis of water is endothermic. It needs a constant supply of electrical energy and stops at once without electricity.
90180.m: Endothermic reactions only run with a constant supply of energy.

90181.q: What does the Greek prefix ‘endo’ in the word endothermic mean?
90181.e: ‘Endo’ means ‘inside’ or ‘in’. In an endothermic reaction, heat goes into the system.
90181.m: Endothermic means that heat goes in.

90182.q: What is meant by activation energy?
a: The energy a reaction needs to start
The energy released at the end
90182.e: For particles to react, bonds must first be loosened. The starting energy needed for this is called activation energy.
90182.m: Activation energy gets a reaction going.

90183.q: Where does the activation energy come from when you strike a match?
a: From the moisture in the air
From the light in the room
From the weight of the match
90183.e: Rubbing the match on the striking surface creates heat. This heat starts the reaction in the match head.
90183.m: The heat of friction can start a reaction.

90184.q: Why does a piece of wood on the table not burn by itself, even though oxygen is there?
90184.e: Burning wood does release energy, but it must be started first. At room temperature there is not enough energy for this.
90184.m: Without starting energy, even burning does not begin.

90185.q: How is activation energy shown in an energy diagram?
a: As an energy hill before the products
As a valley below the starting materials
As an arrow pointing down at the end
90185.e: From the starting materials the curve first rises before it leads to the products. The height of this hill is the activation energy.
90185.m: The activation energy is the energy hill a reaction must get over.

90186.q: What provides the activation energy for combustion in a petrol engine?
a: The spark from the spark plug
90186.e: The spark plug makes an electric spark. It ignites the mixture of petrol vapour and air in the cylinder.
90186.m: In a petrol engine, a spark starts the combustion.

90187.q: Why do many reactions happen faster at higher temperatures?
a: More particles have enough energy to start
90187.e: The warmer it is, the faster the particles move. So more collisions reach the necessary activation energy.
90187.m: Heat helps to reach the activation energy.

90188.q: When does a collision between two particles lead to a reaction?
a: When the particles are the same size
When the particles are standing still
90188.e: Only collisions with at least the activation energy are successful. Weaker collisions make the particles bounce apart unchanged.
90188.m: Only collisions with enough energy lead to a reaction.

90189.q: What does a catalyst do to the energy hill of a reaction?
90189.e: A catalyst lowers the activation energy. This makes the reaction start more easily and run faster.
90189.m: A catalyst lowers the energy hill.

90190.q: What does a catalyst do in a chemical reaction?
a: It speeds it up without being used up
It increases the mass of the products
90190.e: A catalyst makes a reaction run faster. At the end it is still there, unchanged.
90190.m: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up itself.

90191.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
90191.e: The catalyst makes a different reaction path possible, with a smaller energy hill. So more particles react in the same time.
90191.m: A catalyst makes the energy hill smaller.

90192.q: Which poisonous gas does a car's catalytic converter turn into carbon dioxide?
90192.e: Carbon monoxide is very poisonous. In the catalytic converter it reacts with oxygen to form less dangerous carbon dioxide.
90192.m: The catalytic converter turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.

90193.q: Which precious metal works in many catalytic converters?
90193.e: Catalytic converters contain thin layers of platinum, palladium or rhodium. These metals speed up the conversion of the exhaust gases.
90193.m: Platinum is an important metal in the catalytic converter.

90194.q: What are the catalysts in living things called?
90194.e: Enzymes are mostly proteins that speed up reactions in the body. Without them, digestion, for example, would be far too slow.
90194.m: Enzymes are the catalysts of living things.

90195.q: Why does bread taste slightly sweet after you chew it for a long time?
a: An enzyme in saliva splits starch into sugar
The bread gets warm in the mouth
90195.e: Saliva contains an enzyme that splits starch into smaller sugar particles. That is why bread tastes sweetish after long chewing.
90195.m: An enzyme in saliva breaks starch down into sugar.

90196.q: Why does industry use catalysts in many manufacturing processes?
a: The reactions run faster and need less energy
The catalyst becomes the finished product
90196.e: Catalysts speed up reactions, often at lower temperatures too. This saves time, energy and money.
90196.m: Catalysts save time and energy in industry.

90197.q: If you add manganese dioxide to hydrogen peroxide, it foams a lot. Which gas forms?
90197.e: Manganese dioxide acts as a catalyst and speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. This produces water and oxygen.
90197.m: Manganese dioxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

90198.q: Where is the catalytic converter in a car?
90198.e: The catalytic converter is built into the exhaust pipe. The exhaust gases flow through it and are turned into less harmful substances.
90198.m: The catalytic converter cleans the exhaust gases in the exhaust.

90199.q: Why does food go off more slowly in the fridge?
a: There is no air at all in the fridge
The light in the fridge kills germs
90199.e: At low temperatures the particles move more slowly. So breakdown and decay happen more slowly.

90200.q: What usually happens to a chemical reaction when you raise the temperature?
90200.e: At higher temperatures the particles move faster and collide more often. That is why most reactions run faster.

90201.q: Why do wood shavings burn faster than a whole log?
a: They have a larger surface area
90201.e: The more finely a substance is divided, the more particles are at the surface. That is where the oxygen can attack.

90202.q: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. In which acid is it faster?
90202.e: Concentrated acid has more acid particles per volume. So there are more collisions with the metal.
90202.m: A higher concentration speeds up a reaction.

90203.q: What does the rate of reaction tell you?
a: How much the amount of a substance changes per unit of time
90203.e: You measure how much starting material disappears or how much product forms per unit of time. This gives the rate of reaction.
90203.m: The rate of reaction describes the change per unit of time.

90204.q: Why can fine flour dust in the air explode?
a: The huge surface area reacts in a flash
90204.e: Every tiny grain of flour is surrounded by air. A spark can therefore set off an extremely fast combustion, a dust explosion.
90204.m: Fine dust in the air can burn explosively.

90205.q: Why do reactions run faster at higher temperatures?
a: The particles collide more often and harder
90205.e: Warmer particles move faster. There are more collisions, and more of them have enough energy for a reaction.
90205.m: Heat makes particles faster and reactions more frequent.

90206.q: Marble reacts with hydrochloric acid and forms a gas. How can you measure the rate of reaction?
a: Measure the amount of gas produced per minute
Look at the colour of the acid
Measure the length of the glass
90206.e: You collect the gas and read off the volume at fixed time intervals. The more gas per minute, the faster the reaction.
90206.m: The amount of gas per unit of time shows how fast a reaction is.

90207.q: When 10 g of limestone is heated, 5.6 g of quicklime and a gas are produced. How much gas escapes?
90207.e: The total mass stays the same, so the escaping carbon dioxide weighs 10 g minus 5.6 g = 4.4 g.
90207.m: You can work out the mass of an escaping gas from the difference in mass.

90208.q: Matches burn in a sealed jar on a scale. What does the scale show afterwards?
90208.e: In the sealed jar, no gas can escape and none can get in. That is why the mass stays the same.
90208.m: In a sealed container the mass does not change during a reaction.

90209.q: Steel wool is burnt on a scale and is heavier afterwards. Why?
a: The iron has combined with oxygen from the air
90209.e: When it burns, iron combines with oxygen to form iron oxide. The mass of the oxygen is added.
90209.m: When a substance combines with oxygen, it gets heavier.

90210.q: Two substances react completely to form 50 g of product. One of the substances weighed 30 g. How heavy was the other?
90210.e: Both starting materials together must weigh 50 g. So 50 g minus 30 g = 20 g.
90210.m: You can work out the mass of a missing starting material from the mass of the product.

90211.q: 56 g of iron reacts completely with 32 g of sulphur. How much iron sulphide forms?
90211.e: According to the law of conservation of mass: 56 g + 32 g = 88 g of iron sulphide.
90211.m: Add up the masses of the starting materials to get the mass of the product.

90212.q: 12 g of carbon burns completely with 32 g of oxygen. How much carbon dioxide forms?
90212.e: The masses of the starting materials together give the mass of the product: 12 g + 32 g = 44 g.
90212.m: Mass is also conserved when carbon burns.

90213.q: A candle gets lighter as it burns. Where does the mass go?
a: Into gases that escape into the air
90213.e: The wax reacts to form carbon dioxide and water vapour. These gases spread into the air, which is why the scale shows less.
90213.m: When gases escape, a substance seems to get lighter.

90214.q: What must be the same on both sides of a correct chemical equation?
a: The number of each kind of atom
90214.e: In reactions, atoms are only joined up in new ways, not created or destroyed. That is why each kind of atom must appear equally often on the left and right.
90214.m: In a chemical equation, the number of each kind of atom matches on the left and right.

90215.q: Which country did the chemist Antoine de Lavoisier come from?
90215.e: Lavoisier was born in Paris in 1743. He is one of the best-known French scientists.
90215.m: Antoine de Lavoisier was a French chemist.

90216.q: Which old theory about burning did Lavoisier disprove?
90216.e: According to the phlogiston theory, a substance called phlogiston was supposed to escape during burning. Lavoisier showed that burning substances instead combine with a part of the air.
90216.m: Lavoisier explained burning as a reaction with oxygen.

90217.q: What French name did Lavoisier give to oxygen?
90217.e: ‘Oxygène’ means ‘acid former’, because Lavoisier believed the substance was found in all acids. This is also where the chemical symbol O comes from.

90218.q: How did Antoine de Lavoisier die in 1794?
90218.e: Lavoisier collected taxes for the king. During the French Revolution a court sentenced him for this, and he died on the guillotine in Paris.
90218.m: Lavoisier lost his life in the French Revolution.

90219.q: Which measuring instrument was especially important for Lavoisier's experiments?
90219.e: Lavoisier weighed substances very precisely before and after a reaction. In this way he realised that the total mass stays the same.
90219.m: Lavoisier made the precise balance the most important tool in chemistry.

90220.q: As Lavoisier showed, which gas from the air do burning substances combine with?
90220.e: Lavoisier realised that part of the air is used up during burning. He called this substance oxygen.
90220.m: When substances burn, they combine with oxygen.

90221.q: Lavoisier's famous textbook came out in 1789. Which event began in the same year?
a: The founding of the Swiss Confederation
90221.e: The textbook ‘Traité élémentaire de chimie’ came out in 1789. In the same year, citizens in Paris stormed the Bastille.
90221.m: Lavoisier's textbook came out in the year of the French Revolution.

90222.q: What did Lavoisier show about water?
a: It is a compound of two elements
It is an element that cannot be split
90222.e: For a long time water was thought to be a basic element. Lavoisier showed that it can be split and also built up from hydrogen and oxygen.
90222.m: Water is not an element but a compound.

90223.q: Because of his work, what is Antoine de Lavoisier often called?
90223.e: With precise measurements, clear names for substances and the law of conservation of mass, he laid the foundations of today's chemistry.
90223.m: Lavoisier is seen as the founder of modern chemistry.

90224.q: Why are balloons filled with helium today instead of hydrogen?
90224.e: Hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air. Helium is also lighter than air, but it does not burn.
90224.m: Mixed with air, hydrogen catches fire very easily.

90225.q: How do you hold the test tube for the hydrogen pop test?
90225.e: Hydrogen is much lighter than air and would escape upwards out of an open, upright tube. That is why you hold the opening downwards.
90225.m: Because hydrogen is so light, you hold the tube upside down.

90226.q: How can you tell that the hydrogen pop test is positive?
a: By a whistling or squeaky pop sound
90226.e: The gas burns very quickly in the tube. This makes a typical whistle or a short pop.
90226.m: A whistle or pop in the pop test shows hydrogen.

a: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen
A mixture of nitrogen and argon
90227.e: Oxyhydrogen is made of hydrogen and oxygen. Even a small spark makes it react violently.
90227.m: Oxyhydrogen is an explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.

90228.q: Which substance forms when oxyhydrogen reacts?
90228.e: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. After the test you can sometimes see tiny droplets in the tube.

90229.q: In what ratio by volume do hydrogen and oxygen in oxyhydrogen react most violently?
90229.e: A water molecule needs two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. That is why a mixture of two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen reacts most violently.
90229.m: In oxyhydrogen there are two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen.

90230.q: What do you hear when there is almost pure hydrogen in the test tube?
90230.e: Pure hydrogen burns quietly at the opening, because there is hardly any oxygen in the tube. It only whistles loudly when air is mixed in.
90230.m: Pure hydrogen burns with a quiet sound.

90231.q: Which reaction is often used in the school lab to make hydrogen for the pop test?
90231.e: Base metals such as zinc react with hydrochloric acid. Bubbles of hydrogen rise up.
90231.m: Zinc and hydrochloric acid produce hydrogen in the lab.

90232.q: Why must the valves of oxygen cylinders never be lubricated with oil or grease?
a: Oil can catch fire violently in pure oxygen
Oil blocks the cylinder at once
90232.e: In pure oxygen, substances burn much more violently than in air. Oil and grease can even catch fire by themselves there.
90232.m: Pure oxygen and oil are a dangerous mix.

90233.q: What do you see in a positive glowing splint test?
a: The glowing splint bursts into a bright flame
90233.e: In pure oxygen, wood burns much more strongly than in air. That is why the glowing tip relights with a bright flame.
90233.m: A glowing splint that relights shows oxygen.

a: A wooden splint that glows but does not burn
A metal rod with a battery
A small glass tube with gas
90234.e: You light a wooden splint and blow out the flame. What remains is a glowing tip that only smoulders.
90234.m: A glowing splint is a glowing piece of wood without a flame.

90235.q: Why does a glowing splint not relight in normal air?
a: Air contains only about 21 per cent oxygen
90235.e: To relight, the splint needs much more oxygen than there is in normal air. There it just keeps glowing.
90235.m: Normal air has too little oxygen to relight a glowing splint.

90236.q: What happens to a glowing splint in carbon dioxide?
a: It bursts into a bright flame
90236.e: Carbon dioxide does not support burning. The glowing wood lacks oxygen and goes out.
90236.m: A glowing splint goes out in carbon dioxide.

90237.q: What are substances such as oxygen called that strongly help things burn?
90237.e: Oxygen does not burn itself, but it makes burning much more violent. Such substances are called oxidising.
90237.m: Oxygen is not flammable, but it is oxidising.

90238.q: Which hazard symbol is on cylinders of pure oxygen?
90238.e: The symbol with a flame over a circle marks oxidising substances. It warns that fires can become much more violent.
90238.m: A flame over a circle warns of oxidising substances.

90239.q: In the light, water plants form gas bubbles that relight a glowing splint. Which process makes the gas?
90239.e: Photosynthesis produces oxygen as well as glucose. The plant releases it into the water as bubbles.
90239.m: Plants give off oxygen during photosynthesis.

90240.q: Which gas is detected with the limewater test?
90240.e: You bubble the gas through limewater. If it turns cloudy, that shows carbon dioxide.
90240.m: The limewater test detects carbon dioxide.

90241.q: What do you see in a positive limewater test?
a: The limewater turns milky and cloudy
90241.e: Fine white particles form in the clear limewater. This makes the liquid look milky.
90241.m: If limewater turns cloudy, carbon dioxide is present.

a: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water
90242.e: Limewater is made by dissolving slaked lime, that is calcium hydroxide, in water and filtering it. It is clear and colourless.
90242.m: Limewater is clear, dissolved calcium hydroxide.

90243.q: Which substance makes limewater go cloudy in the limewater test?
90243.e: Carbon dioxide reacts with the dissolved calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate. This chalk hardly dissolves and appears as a white cloudiness.
90243.m: In the limewater test, calcium carbonate forms.

90244.q: Roughly how much carbon dioxide does the air you breathe out contain?
90244.e: Air you breathe in contains only about 0.04 per cent carbon dioxide; air you breathe out contains about a hundred times more. That is why limewater goes cloudy quickly when you blow into it through a straw.
90244.m: Breathed-out air contains much more carbon dioxide than breathed-in air.

90245.q: The gases from a candle flame turn limewater cloudy. What does this tell you about the candle wax?
90245.e: The carbon dioxide detected can only form if the fuel contains carbon. The oxygen comes from the air.
90245.m: Carbon dioxide from a flame shows there is carbon in the fuel.

90246.q: Why does limewater go cloudy when you blow into it through a straw?
90246.e: Breathed-out air contains a lot of carbon dioxide. It reacts with the limewater, white chalk forms and the water turns milky.
90246.m: Breathed-out air turns limewater cloudy because it contains carbon dioxide.

90247.q: Is limewater acidic, neutral or alkaline?
90247.e: Calcium hydroxide is a base. Limewater has a pH of about 12 and turns universal indicator blue to violet.

90248.q: When lighting a fire, why does it help to blow gently on the embers?
a: The wind removes the ash as fuel
90248.e: Blowing pushes fresh air onto the glowing parts. With more oxygen, the fire burns more strongly.
90248.m: More oxygen makes a fire burn more strongly.

90249.q: What happens if one side of the fire triangle is missing?
90249.e: All three conditions must be met at the same time. If you remove one of them, burning cannot continue.
90249.m: If one side of the triangle is missing, the fire goes out.

90250.q: Someone pours sand onto a campfire. Which side of the triangle does this remove?
90250.e: The sand covers the embers. No fresh air can reach the fuel any more.
90250.m: Covering a fire smothers it because oxygen is missing.

90251.q: Water is sprayed onto a wood fire. Which condition does this mainly remove?
90251.e: Water takes in a great deal of heat as it warms up and evaporates. The wood cools below its ignition temperature.
90251.m: Water puts out a fire by cooling it.

90252.q: During a forest fire, firefighters cut down trees to make a firebreak. What are they taking away from the fire?
90252.e: In the firebreak there is nothing left that could burn. The fire cannot spread any further there.
90252.m: Without fuel, a fire cannot spread.

90253.q: What is the ignition temperature of a substance?
a: The lowest temperature at which it catches fire by itself
The temperature at which it melts
The temperature at which it freezes
90253.e: Only from its ignition temperature upwards does a substance start burning in air by itself. Every substance has its own ignition temperature.
90253.m: Below its ignition temperature, a substance does not catch fire by itself.

90254.q: You turn off the gas tap on a gas cooker. Why does the flame go out?
90254.e: Without gas flowing in, there is nothing left to burn. The flame goes out at once.
90254.m: Stopping the fuel supply puts out the fire.

90255.q: Why does a candle under an upside-down glass go out after a short time?
a: The oxygen in the glass gets used up
90255.e: The flame uses up the oxygen under the glass. No new air can flow in, so it goes out.
90255.m: A flame constantly needs fresh oxygen.

90256.q: Why must you never put out burning oil in a pan with water?
a: The water turns to steam instantly and throws burning oil out
The water makes the oil colder
The water turns the oil black
The water dissolves the oil at once
90256.e: Water sinks beneath the hot oil and turns to steam explosively. Burning oil sprays everywhere. Instead, you cover the pan with a lid or a fire blanket.
90256.m: Never put out a fat fire with water; cover it instead.

90257.q: Which materials belong to fire class A?
a: Solid materials that form embers, such as wood and paper
90257.e: Fire class A covers solid materials that burn with embers. These include wood, paper, textiles and coal.
90257.m: Wood and paper belong to fire class A.

90258.q: Which fire extinguisher is suitable for computer rooms because it leaves no residue?
90258.e: Carbon dioxide pushes away the oxygen and then evaporates completely. Electrical equipment is not left dirty.
90258.m: A carbon dioxide extinguisher puts out fires cleanly without residue.

90259.q: How does a foam extinguisher put out burning petrol?
a: The foam forms a blanket over the liquid
The foam turns petrol into water
The foam makes the petrol heavier
90259.e: The foam floats on the burning liquid. It separates it from the air and cools it at the same time.
90259.m: A blanket of foam separates burning liquids from the air.

90260.q: Which fire extinguisher works on fire classes A, B and C but leaves a lot of dust?
90260.e: The extinguishing powder works on solids, liquids and gases. Afterwards, though, fine dust lies everywhere and can damage equipment.
90260.m: An ABC powder extinguisher is versatile but makes a lot of mess.

90262.q: What is the best way to put out burning magnesium?
a: With dry sand or metal fire powder
90262.e: Burning metals react violently with water and even with carbon dioxide. Dry sand or special powder smothers the fire safely.
90262.m: Metal fires are put out with dry sand or special powder.

90263.q: Which fire class stands for flammable liquids such as petrol and alcohol?
90263.e: Fire class B covers liquids and substances that become liquid when they burn, such as petrol, alcohol or wax.
90263.m: Burning liquids belong to fire class B.

90264.q: What is the French abbreviation for the Swiss Federal Railways?
90264.e: In French the SBB is called “Chemins de fer fédéraux suisses”, CFF for short. In Italian the abbreviation is FFS.
90264.m: In French the SBB is called CFF.

90265.q: In which year did the Swiss Federal Railways start full operation?
90265.e: On 1 January 1902 the SBB took over operations as a company of its own. Before that, railways in Switzerland were mostly run by private companies.

90266.q: How did the Swiss Federal Railways come about?
a: After a popular vote the Confederation bought up private railways
A rich businessman founded them alone
The cantons merged their postal services
They grew out of a tram in Zurich
90266.e: In 1898 the people voted for the nationalisation of the big private railways. The state railway was then formed from them.
90266.m: The SBB came about through the nationalisation of private railways.

90267.q: What is the Swiss railway station clock famous for around the world?
90267.e: The station clock has black bars instead of numbers and a red second hand. You can read it easily even from far away.
90267.m: The Swiss station clock is simple and easy to read.

90268.q: What does the red second hand of the SBB station clock do at the 12?
90268.e: The hand goes round a little faster than one minute and then waits for about one and a half seconds. Only with the minute pulse do both hands jump on.
90268.m: The second hand of the station clock pauses briefly at the 12.

90269.q: What does the shape of the station clock's red second hand remind you of?
a: The signal disc used by station staff
90269.e: The hand has a round disc at the end. It looks like the signal disc that was used in the past to send trains off.
90269.m: The second hand looks like a signal disc.

90270.q: Which station in Switzerland has the most visitors per day?
90270.e: Zurich main station is the busiest station in the country. In 2023 an average of over 400,000 people got on or off there on a weekday.
90270.m: Zurich HB is the largest station in Switzerland.

90271.q: Roughly how long is the SBB's standard-gauge network (as of 2022)?
90271.e: In 2022 the SBB's standard-gauge network covered about 3265 kilometres. It is fully electrified.
90271.m: The SBB network is over 3000 kilometres long.

90272.q: What does a clock-face timetable mean?
a: Trains leave regularly at the same minute each time
Trains run at different times every day
90272.e: In a clock-face timetable a train leaves, for example, every hour at the same minute. So the timetable repeats itself regularly.
90272.m: In a clock-face timetable trains run at fixed intervals.

90273.q: In which year did Switzerland introduce the nationwide clock-face timetable?
90273.e: In May 1982 the clock-face timetable started on almost all railway lines in the country. It was a big step for public transport.
90273.m: Swiss trains have run to a clock-face timetable since 1982.

a: A station where trains meet so people can change
A knot in the overhead line
90274.e: At a timetable hub, trains from several directions arrive shortly before the hour or half hour. They leave again shortly afterwards, so changing trains works.
90274.m: At a timetable hub, trains meet so people can change.

90275.q: Which of these stations is an important full hub in the Swiss clock-face timetable?
90275.e: Bern, Zurich HB and Basel SBB are full hubs. There, trains from many directions connect with each other.
90275.m: Bern is an important railway hub for changing trains.

90276.q: A train on an hourly timetable leaves at 9.17. When does the train after next leave?
90276.e: On an hourly timetable a train leaves every hour at the same minute. The next one leaves at 10.17, the one after that at 11.17.
90276.m: On an hourly timetable a train leaves every hour at the same minute.

90277.q: What advantage does a clock-face timetable have for passengers?
a: The departure times are easy to remember
You no longer need a ticket
90277.e: Because the departures are the same every hour, they are easy to remember. The connections at the hubs also fit together.
90277.m: A clock-face timetable is easy to remember.

90278.q: A train on a half-hourly timetable leaves at 7.04. When does the next one leave?
90278.e: Half-hourly means every 30 minutes. 7.04 plus 30 minutes makes 7.34.
90278.m: On a half-hourly timetable a train leaves every 30 minutes.

90279.q: Which means of transport was also included in the nationwide clock-face timetable?
90279.e: Not only the trains but many PostBus routes also ran to the clock-face timetable. So buses and trains fit together in many places.
90279.m: The PostBus also runs to the timetable and connects with the trains.

90280.q: What is a marshalling yard for?
a: Sorting goods wagons and making them into new trains
90280.e: Goods wagons come from many places and have different destinations. In the marshalling yard they are sorted by destination and put together again.
90280.m: In a marshalling yard goods wagons are sorted by destination.

90281.q: What is the small hill called that goods wagons roll down in a marshalling yard?
90281.e: A locomotive pushes the wagons onto the hill. Then they roll down one by one by gravity into their track.
90281.m: From the hump the wagons roll into their tracks by themselves.

90282.q: What slows down rolling goods wagons in a marshalling yard?
90282.e: Rail brakes press against the wheels from the side. That way the wagons roll only fast enough to meet the other wagons gently.
90282.m: Rail brakes control the speed of the rolling wagons.

90283.q: Where is Switzerland's most important marshalling yard for single goods wagons?
90283.e: The Limmattal marshalling yard is near Spreitenbach and Dietikon. It is one of the largest and most efficient in Europe.
90283.m: The Limmattal marshalling yard is the most important in Switzerland.

90284.q: Across which two cantons does the Limmattal marshalling yard stretch?
90284.e: One part is in Spreitenbach in the canton of Aargau, the other in Dietikon in the canton of Zurich.
90284.m: The Limmattal marshalling yard is in Aargau and Zurich.

90285.q: What are the many sorting tracks in a marshalling yard for?
a: Wagons with similar destinations collect there
90285.e: Each sorting track stands for one destination. The Limmattal marshalling yard, for example, has 64 such tracks.
90285.m: In the sorting tracks, wagons are collected by destination.

90286.q: What has to be undone between two goods wagons before they can roll down one by one?
90286.e: The wagons are joined by couplings. Only when these are undone can each wagon roll into its track on its own.
90286.m: Before rolling down, the wagons are separated at the coupling.

90287.q: For which kind of goods traffic are marshalling yards especially important?
90287.e: Many companies send only single wagons. These are collected, sorted in the marshalling yard and sent on with other wagons.
90287.m: Single goods wagons are collected and distributed in the marshalling yard.

90288.q: What does a signal box do?
a: Sets and secures points and signals
90288.e: In the signal box, points are switched and signals are operated. The technology makes sure that no train journeys put each other in danger.
90288.m: A signal box controls points and signals.

90289.q: What is the person called who controls train traffic in a signal box?
90289.e: The signaller clears routes and sets the signals. They keep track of where the trains are.
90289.m: The signaller works in the signal box.

90290.q: What moved points and signals in old mechanical signal boxes?
90290.e: The signalman pulled big levers. Long wires or rods then moved the points and signals.
90290.m: Mechanical signal boxes work with levers and wires.

90291.q: What does a modern electronic signal box work with?
90291.e: Electronic signal boxes are operated via screens. Computers check all the safety conditions.
90291.m: Modern signal boxes are controlled by computers.

90292.q: What is the set and secured path for a train through a station called?
90292.e: For a train journey, all the points are set correctly and locked. This secured path is called a route.
90292.m: A route is the secured path of a train.

90293.q: What does the safety technology in a signal box prevent?
a: A signal showing proceed while a set of points is wrong
90293.e: The signal box checks that all points are set correctly and the way is clear. Only then can the signal be set to proceed.
90293.m: A signal box only clears safe routes.

90294.q: From where are many SBB signal boxes operated today?
a: From the cab of every train
By the conductors on the train
90294.e: The SBB controls traffic from a few operations centres. From there, many signal boxes across the country are remotely controlled.
90294.m: Many signal boxes are remotely controlled from operations centres.

90295.q: Which type of signal box works with many electrical switches called relays?
90295.e: In a relay signal box, electric relays handle the safety logic. It is usually operated with buttons on a track diagram.
90295.m: Relay signal boxes secure train journeys with electrical switches.

90296.q: Which two places does the Albula Railway connect?
90296.e: The Albula Railway runs from Thusis via Filisur and Bergün through the Albula Tunnel into the Engadine to St Moritz. It is about 62 kilometres long.
90296.m: The Albula Railway runs from Thusis to St Moritz.

90297.q: Which railway company runs the Albula Railway?
90297.e: The Albula Railway is part of the network of the Rhaetian Railway, RhB for short. This railway runs mainly in the canton of Grisons.
90297.m: The Albula Railway is a line of the Rhaetian Railway.

90298.q: Which honour did the Albula Railway receive together with the Bernina Railway?
a: It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site
It became part of the National Park
It is the longest railway in the world
It is the fastest railway in Europe
90298.e: The Albula and Bernina lines were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site together in 2008. The honour recognises how they were built in a unique landscape.
90298.m: The Albula and Bernina Railways are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

90299.q: The Albula Railway climbs at most 35 per mille. How many metres of height does it gain at most over one kilometre?
90299.e: Per mille means thousandths. 35 per mille of 1000 metres is 35 metres. So the Albula Railway manages without a rack.
90299.m: 35 per mille means a climb of 35 metres in 1 kilometre.

90300.q: Why does the Albula Railway go through spiral tunnels and loops between Bergün and Preda?
a: To gain a lot of height with a gentle gradient
To make the journey last longer
Because a lake is in the way there
90300.e: The difference in height is big over a short distance. Loops and spiral tunnels make the line longer, so ordinary trains can still use it.
90300.m: Spiral tunnels lengthen the line and so reduce the gradient.

90301.q: Why does the Albula Railway go through a tunnel under the Albula Pass instead of over the pass?
a: Because the pass is too high and steep for the railway
Because there is a lake on the pass
Because trains cannot go round bends
Because the pass belongs to Italy
90301.e: A railway without a rack can only climb a little. The Albula Tunnel is almost 6 kilometres long and saves the trains the climb over the high pass.
90301.m: The Albula Tunnel takes the railway under the pass.

90302.q: Why was a new tunnel built next to the old Albula Tunnel?
a: Because the old tunnel was over 100 years old and in poor condition
Because the old tunnel had collapsed
Because a motorway was being built there
90302.e: The old Albula Tunnel was over a hundred years old and badly needed repair. Since 2024 trains have used the new tunnel, and the old one serves as a safety tunnel.
90302.m: Since 2024 trains have used the new Albula Tunnel.

90303.q: What gauge is the Albula Railway?
90303.e: The Rhaetian Railway runs on rails 1000 mm apart. This narrow gauge allows tighter bends in the mountains.
90303.m: The Albula Railway is a metre-gauge railway.

90304.q: Roughly when was the Albula Railway built?
90304.e: The Albula Railway was built between 1898 and 1904. Since 1904 it has run all the way to St Moritz.
90304.m: The Albula Railway is over 100 years old.

90305.q: In which year was the Gotthard Railway opened?
90305.e: From 1 June 1882 the line from Immensee to Chiasso was in operation all the way. It connects German-speaking Switzerland with Ticino.
90305.m: The Gotthard Railway has been running since 1882.

90306.q: Roughly how long is the old Gotthard summit tunnel of the railway?
90306.e: The tunnel between Göschenen and Airolo measures 15,003 metres. When it opened, it was the longest tunnel in the world.
90306.m: The old Gotthard Tunnel is about 15 kilometres long.

90307.q: Which Zurich politician and businessman was the first president of the Gotthard Railway Company?
90307.e: Alfred Escher campaigned hard for the route over the Gotthard. Because of financial problems he stepped down as president in 1879.
90307.m: Alfred Escher was an important supporter of the Gotthard Railway.

90308.q: Why is the church of Wassen famous among railway travellers?
a: You can see it from three levels of the line
It stands in the middle of the tunnel
It sits on a station roof
90308.e: Near Wassen the line winds up the mountain in loops with spiral tunnels. The church appears three times from different angles.
90308.m: You see the church of Wassen three times from the Gotthard Railway.

90309.q: In which year did the Gotthard Base Tunnel start regular timetabled service?
90309.e: After a grand opening in June, trains ran through it regularly from December 2016. Since then the journey to Ticino has been much shorter.
90309.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel has been in service since 2016.

90310.q: From where was the old Gotthard Tunnel built?
a: From Göschenen and Airolo at the same time
90310.e: The workers dug towards each other from both sides at the same time. In February 1880 they met inside the mountain for the breakthrough.
90310.m: The Gotthard Tunnel was dug from both sides.

90311.q: Why was the Gotthard Railway switched from steam to electricity?
a: To stop depending on imported coal
The tunnels were too short for steam locomotives
90311.e: Switzerland has hardly any coal, but lots of hydropower. With electricity from hydropower, the trains ran electrically all the way from 1922.
90311.m: The Gotthard Railway runs on electricity instead of coal.

a: They steer a train onto a different track
90312.e: At a set of points one track splits into two. Depending on how they are set, the train goes straight on or turns off.
90312.m: Points connect tracks and steer trains onto them.

90313.q: What are the moving rail parts of a set of points called?
90313.e: Depending on the setting, the blades lie against one rail or the other. That way they guide the wheels in the right direction.
90313.m: The switch blades decide where a train goes.

90314.q: Why may a train only set off once all the points are set correctly?
a: Otherwise it goes onto the wrong track
90314.e: Wrongly set points can send a train onto an occupied track. That is why the signal box checks all the points before the signal shows proceed.
90314.m: Points must be set correctly before the journey.

90315.q: Why do many points in Switzerland have heating?
a: So that snow and ice do not block the blades
So that the rails do not rust
So that animals can warm up
90315.e: Frozen snow between the blade and the rail stops the points from moving. Point heating keeps them working in winter.
90315.m: Point heaters keep points clear in winter.

90316.q: From where are the points of a large station controlled?
90316.e: In the signal box, specialists or computers set the points and signals. That way all trains run on the right track.
90316.m: Points are controlled from the signal box.

90317.e: A motor next to the points moves the blades. It is controlled from the signal box.
90317.m: Modern points are moved by motors.

90318.q: At a set of points, what decides whether the train goes straight on or turns off?
a: The position of the moving blades
The driver with a steering wheel
90318.e: Trains have no steering wheel. The switch blades lie against a rail and guide the wheels in the right direction.
90318.m: The switch blades decide the direction of travel.

90319.q: Why do trains often have to slow down when turning off over a set of points?
a: The branching track is a tight curve
The points are made of wood
There is no power on the branch
90319.e: On the straight track the train can go fast. The branching track is curved, so a lower speed limit usually applies there.
90319.m: A lower speed often applies on the branching track of points.

90320.q: How does an electric locomotive get its power from the overhead line?
a: Through the pantograph on the roof
Through a battery in the tender
Through solar cells on the sides
Through a cable to the station
90320.e: The pantograph presses up against the contact wire from below. That way the current flows to the motors.
90320.m: The pantograph takes the power from the overhead line.

90321.q: What does the small letter “e” mean in Swiss locomotive names such as Re 460?
90321.e: In the Swiss naming system, the small letter shows the type of drive. An “e” shows an electric locomotive.
90321.m: The “e” in the locomotive name stands for electric.

90322.q: Does the SBB's railway power have the same frequency as the electricity from a socket?
a: No, it has a lower frequency
No, it has a much higher frequency
No, because railway power is direct current from batteries
90322.e: The electricity from a socket has 50 hertz, the SBB's railway power only 16.7 hertz. That is why the railway runs its own power grid.
90322.m: SBB railway power has a lower frequency than household electricity.

90323.q: How does the current flow back from an electric locomotive?
a: Through the wheels and the rails
90323.e: The circuit has to be closed. The current goes through the wheels into the rails and from there back to the substation.
90323.m: The rails serve as the return conductor for railway power.

90324.q: What can many modern electric locomotives do when braking?
a: Feed electricity back into the grid
90324.e: When braking, the motors work as generators. The electricity produced flows back into the overhead line and can be used by other trains.
90324.m: Modern locomotives recover electricity when braking.

90325.q: Which trains does the SBB locomotive Re 460 mainly pull?
90325.e: The Re 460 can go up to 200 km/h. You mainly see it at the front of InterCity trains with double-deck coaches.
90325.m: The Re 460 mainly pulls InterCity trains.

90326.q: Which locomotive family does the SBB locomotive Re 460 belong to?
90326.e: The Re 460 was delivered from 1992 as part of the “Lok 2000” programme. Swiss companies built 119 of them in total.
90326.m: The Re 460 is the SBB's well-known “Lok 2000”.

90327.q: Which energy source does most of the SBB's railway power come from?
90327.e: The SBB owns its own hydroelectric power stations and buys more electricity from hydropower. That is why the railway in Switzerland runs mostly on renewable energy.
90327.m: SBB railway power comes mainly from hydropower.

90328.q: On which mountain line were the SBB's Crocodile locomotives mainly used?
90328.e: The Crocodiles tackled the steep ramps on the Gotthard. That needed a huge amount of pulling power.
90328.m: The Crocodiles were the strong freight locomotives on the Gotthard.

90329.e: The Crocodiles were among the SBB's first large electric locomotives. They got their power from the overhead line.

90330.q: Where can you still see a Crocodile locomotive today?
a: At the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
In the Federal Palace in Bern
On the roof of the National Museum
90330.e: Some Crocodiles have been preserved. You can see them in museums such as the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne or on heritage trips.
90330.m: Some Crocodiles have been preserved to this day.

90331.q: What were the Crocodiles mainly used for?
90331.e: The locomotives were strong, but not fast. Their job was to pull long, heavy goods trains uphill.

90332.q: Why did the locomotive get the nickname “Crocodile”?
a: Its long, flat bonnets look like a crocodile
It often ran along the water
It was covered in crocodile leather
90332.e: The locomotive has two long bonnets and a middle section. This shape looks like the head, body and tail of a crocodile.
90332.m: The name “Crocodile” comes from the locomotive's long, flat shape.

90333.q: Why is the Crocodile built from several parts joined together?
a: So it can go round tight bends
So it is easier to wash
So it is faster in reverse
90333.e: Such a long, rigid locomotive would not get round the tight bends of the mountain line well. The joints make it more flexible.
90333.m: The joints help the long Crocodile take bends.

90334.q: What does “6/8” mean in the name Ce 6/8?
a: 6 driven axles out of 8 in total
90334.e: In the Swiss naming system the first number gives the driven axles, the second all the axles. So the Crocodile has 8 axles, 6 of which are driven.
90334.m: On the Ce 6/8, 6 of the 8 axles are driven.

90335.q: How is the power of the motors passed to the wheels on the Crocodile?
a: Through a chain like on a bike
90335.e: The motors drive a shaft, and the power goes to the wheels through rods. The turning rods are a typical feature of the locomotive.
90335.m: The Crocodile passes power to the wheels with rods.

90336.q: Which locomotives on the Gotthard were replaced by electric locomotives like the Crocodile?
90336.e: Until around 1920 steam locomotives ran on the Gotthard. Electric locomotives like the Crocodile replaced them because electricity from hydropower was plentiful in Switzerland.
90336.m: On the Gotthard, electric locomotives replaced steam.

90337.q: What is the Pilatus Railway famous for around the world?
a: It is the steepest rack railway in the world
It is the longest cable car in the world
It is the fastest railway in the world
90337.e: The Pilatus Railway climbs up to 48 per cent. The engineer Eduard Locher developed his own rack system for it.
90337.m: The Pilatus Railway is the steepest rack railway in the world.

90338.q: What is the maximum gradient of the Pilatus Railway?
90338.e: At the steepest point the railway rises 48 metres over 100 metres of horizontal distance. That is extremely steep for a rack railway.
90338.m: The Pilatus Railway climbs up to 48 per cent.

90339.q: In which village is the valley station of the Pilatus Railway?
90339.e: The rack railway starts in Alpnachstad on Lake Alpnach. From Kriens, by contrast, a cable car goes up Pilatus.
90339.m: The Pilatus Railway starts in Alpnachstad.

90340.q: What is special about the Pilatus Railway's rack system?
a: The cogwheels grip the rack from the sides
The rack hangs in the air
There are no cogwheels at all
The cogwheels are made of wood
90340.e: Horizontal cogwheels grip the rack from both sides. That way they cannot climb out of the rack on the steep gradient.
90340.m: In the Locher system the cogwheels grip from the side.

90341.q: What did the Pilatus Railway run on before it became electric?
90341.e: At first steam locomotives ran on the Pilatus Railway. Since 1937 it has run on electricity.
90341.m: The Pilatus Railway used to run on steam.

90342.q: In which canton is the valley station of the Pilatus Railway?
90342.e: Alpnachstad is part of the municipality of Alpnach in the canton of Obwalden. Pilatus itself lies on the border of several cantons.
90342.m: The valley station of the Pilatus Railway is in Obwalden.

90343.q: The Pilatus Railway is a narrow-gauge railway. What does that mean?
a: The rails are closer together than on the SBB
The railway runs on only one track
The rails are made of wood
90343.e: On the Pilatus Railway the rails are 800 millimetres apart. On the SBB it is 1435 millimetres.
90343.m: On a narrow-gauge railway the rails are closer together.

90344.q: Roughly how much height does the Pilatus Railway climb?
90344.e: There are 1635 metres of height between the valley and summit stations. Yet the line is only just over 4.6 kilometres long.
90344.m: The Pilatus Railway climbs more than 1600 metres.

90345.q: How does a typical funicular work?
a: Two cars hang on the same cable and balance each other
A car floats through the air on a cable
A cogwheel pulls the car uphill
A steam locomotive pushes the car
90345.e: When one car goes up, the other comes down. Because their weights roughly balance, little driving power is needed.
90345.m: On a funicular two cars balance each other on the cable.

90346.q: Where do the two cars of a single-track funicular pass each other?
a: At the passing loop in the middle
Nowhere, they travel one above the other
90346.e: Roughly in the middle the track splits briefly into two. That is where the cars pass each other.
90346.m: The cars of a funicular pass each other in the middle.

90347.q: What is special about the Abt switch used on funiculars?
a: It needs a lot of electricity
90347.e: The cars have wheels with two flanges on one side and wide wheels on the other. So each car automatically always takes its own side of the passing loop.
90347.m: The Abt switch works without any moving parts.

90348.q: Where is the drive on most funiculars?
a: In the middle of the line
Under the valley station in the water
90348.e: An electric motor in the summit station drives the big cable wheel. The cable that both cars hang from runs over it.
90348.m: The drive of a funicular is usually at the top.

90349.q: How were many early funiculars driven without a motor?
a: With water as ballast in the upper car
90349.e: At the top, a tank in the car was filled with water. The heavier car went down and pulled the lighter one up.
90349.m: Some funiculars used to move with water ballast.

90350.q: How steep is the Stoos funicular near Schwyz at its steepest point?
90350.e: The Stoos funicular, opened in 2017, climbs up to 110 per cent, which is about 48 degrees. It is considered the steepest funicular in the world.
90350.m: The Stoos funicular is one of the steepest funiculars in the world.

90351.q: The Giessbach funicular on Lake Brienz is the oldest funicular still running in Switzerland. Since when has it been running?
90351.e: The Giessbach funicular runs from Lake Brienz to the Grandhotel Giessbach. It has been in operation since 1879.
90351.m: The Giessbach funicular has been running since 1879.

90352.q: Who decided in 1987 whether Switzerland would carry out the Rail 2000 plan?
a: Only the head of the SBB
90352.e: On 6 December 1987 the Swiss people voted on Rail 2000 and said yes. In Switzerland the people often decide directly on big projects.
90352.m: The Swiss people said yes to Rail 2000 in a referendum.

90353.q: What does it mean when trains run to a regular interval timetable, as Rail 2000 introduced?
a: They run at regular intervals, for example every half hour
They always go as fast as a car
They stop twice at every stop
90353.e: In a regular interval timetable trains always leave at the same minute, for example every half hour or hour. That makes the departure times easy to remember.
90353.m: In a regular interval timetable trains run at regular intervals.

90354.q: What did the first stage of Rail 2000 bring passengers in 2004?
90354.e: With the timetable change in December 2004, more trains ran and many connections became faster. It was one of the biggest timetable changes in Switzerland.
90354.m: Rail 2000 brought more trains and faster connections.

90355.q: Since Rail 2000, roughly how long do the fastest trains take from Bern to Zurich?
90355.e: The journey time fell from 69 to 58 and later to 56 minutes. This was made possible mainly by the new line across the Central Plateau.
90355.m: Since Rail 2000 the journey from Bern to Zurich takes under an hour.

90356.q: Which principle describes the aim of Rail 2000?
a: As fast as necessary, not as fast as possible
Each train runs only once a day
90356.e: The trains were not meant to set records, but to reach the hubs on time. That way the connections fit together everywhere.
90356.m: With Rail 2000, good connections count for more than top speed.

90357.q: Why does the train driver see the signals on a screen in the cab at 200 km/h?
a: Because at that speed signals beside the track can hardly be seen in time
Because signals beside the track are banned
Because a screen is cheaper than a lamp
Because the train never runs at night
90357.e: At high speed the signals beside the track fly past too fast. That is why the ETCS system shows the driver all the information directly in the cab.
90357.m: At high speed ETCS shows the signals in the cab.

90358.q: Why should the journey time between two big hubs be just under an hour with Rail 2000?
a: So that the trains make the connections at both hubs
So that the staff can take a break
So that no goods trains can run
90358.e: At the hubs the trains meet on the hour. If the journey time between them is just under an hour, changing trains works at both stations.
90358.m: Journey times under Rail 2000 are matched to the hubs.

90359.q: What is the area under the graph of y = 1/x between x = 1 and x = e?
90359.e: The area is the integral of 1/x from 1 to e, i.e. ln(e) − ln(1) = 1 − 0 = 1. This also lets you define e geometrically.
90359.m: Under the hyperbola 1/x, the area between 1 and e is exactly 1.

90360.q: After which mathematician, born in Basel, is the number e named?
90360.e: Leonhard Euler (1707 to 1783) came from Basel and was the first to use the letter e for this constant. He is considered one of the most productive mathematicians in history.
90360.m: The number e bears the name of Leonhard Euler from Basel.

90361.q: Letters are put into their envelopes completely at random. With many letters, what value does the probability that no letter ends up in the right envelope approach?
90361.e: This problem of permutations without fixed points was already studied by Pierre Rémond de Montmort. The probability tends to 1/e ≈ 0.368.
90361.m: The probability that no letter ends up right is about 1/e.

90362.q: 1 franc earns 100 % interest for one year, with the interest credited monthly. Roughly how much money do you have after one year?
90362.e: You calculate (1 + 1/12)^12 ≈ 2.613. With ever shorter interest periods the amount approaches e ≈ 2.718 without exceeding it.
90362.m: The more often interest is compounded, the closer you get to the number e.

90363.q: What special property does the function f(x) = e^x have when differentiated?
90363.e: For f(x) = e^x, f'(x) = e^x. That is why the exponential function plays a central role in growth and decay processes.
90363.m: The exponential function stays the same when differentiated.

90364.q: Which curve does a freely hanging chain form, described with exponential functions?
90364.e: A hanging chain follows the curve y = a · cosh(x/a), and cosh is made up of e^x and e^(−x). Galileo wrongly thought it was a parabola.
90364.m: A hanging chain forms a catenary, not a parabola.

90365.q: What kind of number is e, as Charles Hermite proved in 1873?
90365.e: Hermite showed that e is not a root of any polynomial with integer coefficients. So e is transcendental and in particular irrational.
90365.m: The number e is transcendental, as Hermite proved in 1873.

90366.q: Which equation is called Euler’s identity?
90366.e: Euler’s identity links the five important numbers e, i, π, 1 and 0. It follows from the formula e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x for x = π.
90366.m: Euler’s identity links e, i, π, 1 and 0 in a single equation.

90367.q: Which infinite sum gives the number e?
90367.e: The sum of the reciprocals of all factorials converges very quickly to e. The harmonic series diverges, the geometric series gives 2 and the Leibniz series gives π/4.
90367.m: The sum of the reciprocals of all factorials gives the number e.

90368.q: Which two basic building blocks make up a graph in graph theory?
90368.e: A graph consists of vertices (nodes) and edges, each connecting two vertices. Graphs can model road networks or friendships, for example.
90368.m: A graph consists of vertices connected by edges.

90369.q: How many edges does the complete graph with 6 vertices have, in which every vertex is connected to every other?
90369.e: A complete graph with n vertices has n · (n − 1) / 2 edges. For n = 6 that gives 6 · 5 / 2 = 15.
90369.m: The complete graph with n vertices has n times (n − 1) divided by two edges.

90370.q: A graph has 12 edges. What is the sum of all vertex degrees?
90370.e: By the handshaking lemma, each edge counts at two vertices. So the degree sum is 2 · 12 = 24.
90370.m: The sum of all vertex degrees is always twice the number of edges.

90371.q: How many edges does a tree with 10 vertices have?
90371.e: A tree is a connected graph without cycles. It always has exactly one more vertex than edges, so 10 − 1 = 9 edges.
90371.m: A tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges.

90372.q: What does the four colour theorem state?
a: Every flat map can be coloured with four colours
Every graph has at most four vertices
90372.e: The countries of any flat map can be coloured with at most four colours so that neighbouring countries have different colours. Appel and Haken proved this in 1976.
90372.m: Four colours are enough for any flat map.

90373.q: What was new and controversial about the proof of the four colour theorem in 1976?
a: It was carried out with computer help
It was only one page long
It was found by an amateur
90373.e: Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken had a computer check a very large number of individual cases. It was the first major mathematical proof that could hardly be checked without a computer.
90373.m: The four colour theorem was the first big proof done with computer help.

90374.q: What do you call a cycle in a graph that visits every vertex exactly once?
90374.e: A Hamiltonian cycle visits all vertices exactly once and returns to the start. An Eulerian circuit, on the other hand, uses every edge exactly once.
90374.m: A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once.

90375.q: Which well-known optimisation problem looks for the shortest round trip through all cities?
90375.e: The travelling salesman problem asks for a shortest Hamiltonian cycle. For many cities it requires an enormous amount of computation.
90375.m: The travelling salesman problem looks for the shortest round trip through all places.

90376.q: What is a graph called that can be drawn in the plane without edges crossing?
90376.e: A planar graph can be drawn so that no edges cross. The complete graph with 5 vertices, for example, is not planar.
90376.m: A planar graph can be drawn without crossings.

90377.q: How many bridges played a role in the Königsberg bridge problem?
90377.e: The bridges in Königsberg connected four areas of land across the River Pregel. The aim was a walk that crosses every bridge exactly once.
90377.m: The Königsberg bridge problem was about seven bridges.

90378.q: In which year did Leonhard Euler show that the Königsberg bridge problem has no solution?
90378.e: Euler proved in 1736 that there is no such walk. His paper on it appeared a few years later in the publications of the St Petersburg Academy.
90378.m: Euler solved the Königsberg bridge problem in 1736.

90379.q: What was the result of the Königsberg bridge problem?
a: The walk is only possible at night
90379.e: There is no walk that crosses every bridge exactly once. This is due to the number of bridges ending at each area of land.
90379.m: In Königsberg you could not cross every bridge exactly once.

90380.q: Why is no walk over all the bridges possible in Königsberg?
a: All four areas of land have odd degree
The bridges are of different lengths
The river has too many islands
90380.e: Anyone passing through an area of land needs one bridge in and one bridge out. But in Königsberg an odd number of bridges led to each area of land, so it does not work out.
90380.m: Too many vertices with odd degree prevent an Eulerian path.

90381.q: What is the maximum number of vertices with odd degree a connected graph may have for an Eulerian path to exist?
90381.e: An Eulerian path exists exactly when 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. With 2 such vertices, the path starts and ends there.
90381.m: An Eulerian path needs 0 or 2 vertices with odd degree.

90382.q: A connected graph has exactly two vertices with odd degree. Where must an Eulerian path start?
a: At one of the two vertices with odd degree
At any vertex with even degree
At the vertex with the most edges
There is then no Eulerian path
90382.e: At every stop along the way you need as many edges in as out, so even degree. Only start and finish may have odd degree, so the path starts at one of these vertices and ends at the other.
90382.m: An Eulerian path starts and ends at the vertices with odd degree.

90383.q: What is the city of Königsberg called today?
90383.e: Königsberg in East Prussia passed to the Soviet Union in 1945 and has been called Kaliningrad since 1946. Today the city belongs to Russia.
90383.m: The former Königsberg is now called Kaliningrad.

90384.q: Which river flowed through Königsberg and formed the areas of land in the bridge problem?
90384.e: The Pregel divided Königsberg into several areas of land, including the island of Kneiphof. The bridges crossed its branches.
90384.m: The Königsberg bridges crossed the Pregel.

90385.q: Which branch of mathematics is considered to have been founded by the Königsberg bridge problem?
90385.e: Euler represented areas of land as points and bridges as connections. This abstraction is the basic idea of graph theory.
90385.m: Graph theory began with the Königsberg bridge problem.

90386.q: What does game theory, founded by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern in 1944, study?
a: Decisions whose outcome also depends on how others behave
The chances of winning at casino games
The rules of board and card games
90386.e: Game theory describes situations in which several parties make decisions and each one’s success also depends on the others. It is applied in economics, politics and biology.
90386.m: Game theory studies decisions whose outcome also depends on how others behave.

90387.q: What does a Nash equilibrium describe?
a: Nobody can do better by changing strategy alone
All players receive the same amount
The total gain is at its maximum
90387.e: In a Nash equilibrium each strategy is the best response to the strategies of the others. A one-sided change gives nobody an advantage.
90387.m: In a Nash equilibrium it does not pay for anyone to deviate alone.

90388.q: Which award did John Nash receive in 1994 for his work on game theory?
90388.e: John Nash received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994 together with John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten. His life was told in the film “A Beautiful Mind”.
90388.m: John Nash was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics for game theory.

90389.q: What do you call a game in which one player’s gain exactly equals the other’s loss?
90389.e: In a zero-sum game the gains and losses of all players add up to zero. Chess or rock, paper, scissors are examples.
90389.m: In a zero-sum game one player’s gain is the other’s loss.

90390.q: Which mixed strategy forms the Nash equilibrium in rock, paper, scissors?
90390.e: If you play each option at random with 1/3, your opponent cannot exploit this strategy. A pure strategy, on the other hand, would be easy to beat.
90390.m: In rock, paper, scissors the equilibrium is to play everything at random with equal probability.

a: It is always best, whatever the opponent does
It is certain to win every game
It is chosen by the stronger player
It is the strategy chosen first
90391.e: A dominant strategy gives at least as much as any other for every possible choice of the other players. Rational players therefore always choose it.
90391.m: A dominant strategy is the best choice regardless of how others behave.

90392.q: According to the minimax principle, a cautious player chooses his strategy in a zero-sum game. What does he do?
a: He keeps his largest possible loss as small as possible
He always aims for the largest possible gain
He chooses every strategy equally often
90392.e: With the minimax principle you plan for the worst case and choose the strategy where it is least bad. John von Neumann proved in 1928 that such games always have an equilibrium with mixed strategies.
90392.m: Under the minimax principle you keep the worst possible loss as small as possible.

90393.q: What is the game called in which two drivers race towards each other and whoever swerves loses?
90393.e: In chicken, the worst outcome is when neither swerves. It has two pure Nash equilibria, in each of which exactly one player swerves.
90393.m: In chicken, the collision is the worst result for both.

90394.q: What kind of game is the prisoner’s dilemma?
90394.e: Depending on their decisions, both together do better or worse. So gains and losses do not simply cancel each other out.
90394.m: In the prisoner’s dilemma the combined outcome is not always the same; it is not a zero-sum game.

90395.q: If both stay silent, both get 1 year. If both confess, both get 4 years. If only one confesses, he goes free and the other gets 6 years. How many years do both get together in the Nash equilibrium?
90395.e: Confessing is dominant: against silence 0 instead of 1, against confessing 4 instead of 6 years. In equilibrium both confess, together 4 + 4 = 8 years.
90395.m: The equilibrium in the prisoner’s dilemma is worse for both together than staying silent together.

90396.q: Why is the outcome of the prisoner’s dilemma considered not Pareto optimal?
a: Both could be better off at the same time
90396.e: If both stayed silent, both would be better off than in the equilibrium. A state in which everyone could be better off is not Pareto optimal.
90396.m: In the prisoner’s dilemma, individually rational behaviour leads to a worse result for everyone.

90397.q: Which area of mathematics does the prisoner’s dilemma belong to?
90397.e: Game theory studies decisions whose outcome also depends on the decisions of others. The prisoner’s dilemma is its best-known example.
90397.m: The prisoner’s dilemma is a classic of game theory.

90398.q: Why do both usually confess in the prisoner’s dilemma, even though staying silent together would be better for both?
a: Confessing pays for each, whatever the other does
Staying silent is against the law
90398.e: Confessing is a dominant strategy: each individual does better with it, regardless of the other’s decision. Together, though, both end up with a worse result.
90398.m: In the prisoner’s dilemma, sensible individual behaviour leads to a worse result for everyone.

90399.q: Which strategy won Robert Axelrod’s computer tournament on the repeated prisoner’s dilemma?
90399.e: Tit for Tat, submitted by Anatol Rapoport, won Axelrod’s tournaments around 1980. It is simple, friendly and retaliatory all at once.
90399.m: In the repeated prisoner’s dilemma, Tit for Tat was particularly successful.

90400.q: How does the Tit for Tat strategy work?
a: Cooperate first, then copy the opponent’s last move
Always do the opposite of the opponent
After any betrayal, betray for ever
90400.e: Tit for Tat starts by cooperating and then always plays what the opponent played in the previous round. So it rewards cooperation and punishes betrayal at once.
90400.m: Tit for Tat starts friendly and then responds as the opponent did before.

90401.q: Which real conflict is often given as an example of a prisoner’s dilemma?
a: An arms race between two states
90401.e: In an arms race, disarmament on both sides would be better for both. But because arming brings each side advantages, both often arm.
90401.m: The arms race shows how the prisoner’s dilemma also arises between states.

90402.e: Benoît Mandelbrot derived the word from the Latin “fractus” (broken). He made fractals famous worldwide with computer graphics.
90402.m: Benoît Mandelbrot invented the word fractal in 1975.

90403.q: Which property is typical of many fractals?
90403.e: Self-similar fractals look like the whole again in enlarged sections. Their dimension is often not a whole number.
90403.m: A part of a fractal often looks like the whole fractal.

90404.q: In the Koch curve, every line segment is replaced at each step by 4 segments, each a third as long. How long is a curve that starts at 9 cm after two steps?
90404.e: At each step the length is multiplied by 4/3. After two steps: 9 · 4/3 · 4/3 = 16 cm.
90404.m: The Koch curve gets longer by a factor of 4/3 at each step.

90405.q: The Koch curve consists of 4 copies of itself, each reduced to a third. Its fractal dimension is log 4 / log 3. Roughly how large is it?
90405.e: log 4 / log 3 ≈ 0.602 / 0.477 ≈ 1.26. So the Koch curve is more than a line, but less than a surface.
90405.m: The Koch curve has a dimension of about 1.26.

90406.q: The Sierpinski triangle consists of 3 copies of itself, each reduced by half. Its fractal dimension is log 3 / log 2. Roughly how large is it?
90406.e: log 3 / log 2 ≈ 0.477 / 0.301 ≈ 1.58. So the Sierpinski triangle lies between a line and a surface.
90406.m: The Sierpinski triangle has a dimension of about 1.58.

90407.q: In the Sierpinski triangle, a quarter of each triangle’s area is removed at every step. What fraction of the area remains after 3 steps?
90407.e: At each step 3/4 of the area remains. After three steps: (3/4)^3 = 27/64.
90407.m: In the Sierpinski triangle the area shrinks to three quarters at each step.

90408.q: What question did Mandelbrot ask in 1967 in the title of a famous paper on fractals in nature?
a: How long is the coast of Britain?
How high is the highest mountain?
90408.e: The measured length of a coastline depends on the scale: the smaller the measuring stick, the longer it becomes. This is typical of fractal shapes.
90408.m: The length of a coastline depends on the scale of measurement, because coastlines are fractal.

90409.q: Which vegetable is often shown as an example of a fractal in nature?
90409.e: In romanesco, each floret is made of smaller florets with the same spiral shape. This self-similarity repeats over several levels.
90409.m: Romanesco shows self-similarity like a fractal.

90410.q: Which iteration rule defines the Mandelbrot set (starting at z = 0)?
90410.e: For each complex number c you iterate z² + c, starting with 0. If the sequence stays bounded, c belongs to the Mandelbrot set.
90410.m: The Mandelbrot set comes from repeatedly squaring and adding c.

90411.q: Which number c belongs to the Mandelbrot set?
90411.e: For c = −1 you get the sequence 0, −1, 0, −1, ..., which stays bounded. For c = 1 you get 0, 1, 2, 5, 26, ... and the sequence grows without bound.
90411.m: Only numbers c whose sequence stays bounded belong to the Mandelbrot set.

90412.q: What is z₃ in the Mandelbrot iteration for c = 1 if z₀ = 0?
90412.e: z₁ = 0² + 1 = 1, z₂ = 1² + 1 = 2, z₃ = 2² + 1 = 5. The sequence keeps growing, so 1 does not belong to the set.
90412.m: In the Mandelbrot iteration you square the last value and add c.

90413.q: Because of its shape, what is the Mandelbrot set often called in German-speaking countries?
90413.e: The main figure consists of a heart-shaped cardioid with a circle attached. This is reminiscent of a little man made of apples.
90413.m: In German the Mandelbrot set is also called Apfelmännchen because of its shape.

90414.q: From which modulus of z can you be sure that the sequence will not stay bounded?
90414.e: If the modulus of z exceeds 2, the sequence is certain to grow to infinity. That is why computer programs stop the calculation there.
90414.m: As soon as the modulus of z is greater than 2, c does not belong to the Mandelbrot set.

90415.q: In which number plane is the Mandelbrot set shown?
90415.e: The values c are complex numbers and are shown in the complex plane with real and imaginary parts. Each pixel corresponds to one c.
90415.m: The Mandelbrot set lies in the plane of complex numbers.

90416.q: How does the Mandelbrot sequence new z equals z² + c run for c = −2 if you start at z = 0?
90416.e: z₁ = 0² − 2 = −2, z₂ = (−2)² − 2 = 2, z₃ = 2² − 2 = 2. The sequence stays at 2 and is bounded, so −2 belongs to the Mandelbrot set. It is its leftmost point on the real axis.
90416.m: The number −2 is the leftmost point of the Mandelbrot set.

90417.q: At which company did Benoît Mandelbrot work when he studied fractals with computers?
90417.e: Mandelbrot did research for many years at IBM’s Thomas J. Watson Research Center. The computing power there let him display complicated sets.
90417.m: Mandelbrot studied fractals as a researcher at IBM.

90418.q: What is left when you cut a square off a golden rectangle along its short side?
90418.e: With a golden rectangle, the remaining rectangle has the same aspect ratio φ. Repeating this produces the golden spiral.
